articles.body:
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain

The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning.

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

The statements are very similar, I’ve pulled out a few below:

Saudi Arabia’sMinistry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement published by the Saudi Press Agency:

The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on the Qatar news agency (QNA):

The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.

I’m going to wrap up coverage for now. Here’s a summary of what you need to know as Iran steps up strikes against US allies in the Gulf again.

Iran launched a six-drone attack on a US airbase in Bahrain early on Sunday, prompting fears of a return to full-blown fighting after a two-month lull in strikes

Bahrain said it had intercepted “several aerial attacks” and destroyed the drones before they reached their targets, and officials did not immediately disclose any damage or injuries

However the tiny Gulf kingdom, which hosts a major US naval command, was forced to send out public warnings and sound missile warning sirens ahead of the incoming strikes

Iran said it had targeted a radar facility at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base. The US is yet to respond, but said there had been no damage from the first attempted strike on Friday.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have claimed the sinking of an oil supertanker which hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. There’s no independent verification of this yet.

The US military had claimed recently that it had cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.

But the IRGC said Sunday that two ships had hit its mines while travelling through the strait, “resulting in massive explosions and fire”.

It said the super tanker had been carrying more than two million barrels of oil when it sunk in the Gulf. Iran has made several announcements in recent weeks about ships hitting mines.

Tehran has heavily restricted shipping traffic through the strait since the start of the war, demanding vessels seek permission and travel via designated pathways. It has fired on ships trying to circumvent Iranian detection.

The US has been supporting ships going through the strait. In the past 24 hours, Centcomm posted on X a picture of F-16 fighter jets and said that more than 1.7 billions of crude oil “have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Gulf partners with U.S. protection.”

As I mentioned earlier, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have said its strikes this morning were retaliation for US aggression.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a press conference in Tehran on Sunday that Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states.

He was asked whether the strike on Tehran, the second this weekend, showed a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled.

Mr. Baghaei said that Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.

The US has launched strikes on Iranian naval bases in the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as well as along Iran’s southern coast. This has been seen as efforts to try and degrade Iran’s striking capability as well as offering cover for commerical ships still venturing through and out of Hormuz.

President Trump has refrained from major military escalation, describing those sporadic strikes as minor. However, American media have reported that both the US and Israel have discussed plans for a fuller resumption of strikes.

Here’s a map showing Bahrain, the smallest Gulf state, in relation to Iran and the rest of its Gulf neighbours. Tehran sent a flurry of drones across the Gulf in the early hours of Sunday morning to target a US air base south of Manama.

Bahrain is home to a major US military base, the NSA Bahrain (or Naval Support Activity Bahrain), which are headquarters for the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, and also acts as key hub of support for all operations in the region.

However the base was struck heavily during Iran’s retaliatory strikes at the start of the war, and it’s unclear whether it’s fully recovered.

American media have reported major damage to its headquarters, barracks and radar facilities.

Iran’s drones this morning were aimed at a different target- the US air base in Al-Rifaa, south of the capital.

The US has formal bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, and access arrangements to military facilities in the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Saudi Arabia.

In light of Iran’s latest strike attempts on US allies in the Gulf, it’s useful to look at what the US commander-in-chief has been saying in recent days, as my colleague Patrick Wintour reports.

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews since Thursday that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Five killed in Houthi attack near Yemeni government capital

I reported earlier that Yemeni government forces are falling back to Aden to try and secure their interim capital which is coming under pressure from Houthi forces.

A Houthi attack on a checkpoint near Aden has killed five people and injured eight others near Aden, AFP is reporting.

The missile targeted a checkpoint in Khor Omeira, Lahj province, AFP says, citing three unnamed military sources and a government source.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain

The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning.

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

The statements are very similar, I’ve pulled out a few below:

Saudi Arabia’sMinistry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement published by the Saudi Press Agency:

The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on the Qatar news agency (QNA):

The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.

Below is the full statement from Bahrain’s foreign ministry on the Iranian drone strikes today, which were intercepted and shot down. This has been published in Bahrain’s various state-controlled media outlets.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression against its territory, including the attack launched today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, by drones that were intercepted and destroyed by air defense systems in the Kingdom’s airspace.

This comes two days after a similar attack at dawn on Friday, November 13, 2026, by two drones that were also intercepted. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression.

The Ministry considered these attacks a resumption of Iran’s heinous aggression against the Kingdom and countries in the region, disregarding the provisions of international law and the principles of the UN Charter.

The Kingdom views them as a blatant attack on its sovereignty and territorial integrity, a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on the Kingdom of Bahrain and neighboring countries and demanded their immediate cessation, a targeting of innocent citizens and residents, a sabotage of de-escalation efforts, and a serious threat to the region’s security and stability.

The Ministry affirmed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s categorical rejection of the flimsy pretexts and baseless claims put forward by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard, emphasizing that no pretext justifies aggression against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.

It stressed that freedom of navigation and passage, by sea and air, in straits used for international navigation is a right guaranteed by the rules of international law and is not subject to the will or conditions of any state.

The Kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.

The Ministry also affirmed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s inherent right, both individually and collectively, to self-defense in accordance with Article (51) of the Charter, and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents, in close coordination with its brothers in the Gulf Cooperation Council, based on the Joint Defense Agreement, which considers an attack on any member state an attack on all, as well as with its allies and partners. The Ministry noted that the Kingdom of Bahrain, as a member of the UN Security Council, calls upon the Council to condemn these repeated attacks and demands that it assume its responsibilities and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817, and to halt its attacks, threats, and support for proxy groups in the region. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs added that the Kingdom of Bahrain affirms that its security is a red line, that its sovereignty is non-negotiable, and that it will remain, as it has always been, a proponent of good neighborliness, respect for the sovereignty of states, and non-interference in their affairs, and is committed to the security and stability of the Arabian Gulf.

Iranian media are reporting that their foreign minister Abbas Araqchi will be in Oman on Tuesday for talks with his Omani counterpart.

Oman, along with Qatar, has been one of the key negotiators in ceasefire and peace talks between Tehran and Washington.

As both sides have settled into a strategy of exerting continued economic pain on the other, we’re yet to see any movement on a deal though.

The US is maintaining a highly expensive military operation in the Gulf, with a naval blockade that aims to stop Iranian oil ships leaving the Persian Gulf, thereby hurting the Iranian economy, and through a missile and drone operation targeting Iran’s southern coastline aimed at protecting and helping commercial ships get out. Oil flows are said to be back near their prewar level.

But Iran hasn’t strayed from its demands, and the conditions it wants to end the war: a measure of control over Hormuz, removal of the blockade and economic sanctions, having its assets unfrozen, and reparations.

Yemen government forces dropping back from Bab el-Mandeb to shore up Aden capital

I mentioned earlier the withdrawal of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces from the areas around Bab el-Mandeb where they’ve been attempting to stave off the Houthis.

A lightning-strike offensive back in September saw the Houthis sweep almost the entire Red Sea coast and almost seize control of the critical Red Sea strait, which has become another chokepoint in the flow of oil and and energy supplies from Gulf producers.

Here’s the full statement from the Yemeni forces, who are now redeploying towards Aden, where their government is based.

The Houthis are gathering steam in the south, where most areas remain under government control.

The Souther Yemeni forces said:

The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate.

This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.

The Houthis’ stronghold currently remains most of northern Yemen, where they control the capital Sanaa and other populous areas. Since the civil war erupted in 2014, the Houthis have pushed the internationally-recognised Yemeni government south and stunned the Saudi-backed administration with their push south in September.

That prompted a military fight back operation, and Saudi Arabia striking Houthi areas in Yemen as the Houthis targeted airports and oil supplies in the Gulf kingdom.

The US thinks Iran still has between 1,500-2,500 missiles in its arsenal despite the US-Israeli damage done this year to its production facilities, reports the Wall St Journal.

They noted difficulties with tracking Iran’s stockpile, and assessing whether they’re ready for launch or remain in storage.

But they noted that Iran has appeared to manage to slowly rebuild its arsenal during the long lulls in fighting and mostly from stockpiled weapons components. Tehran has also kept up a ready supply of drones and short-range missiles.

The assessment would go against what Trump and his Secretary of Defence/War, Peter Hegseth, have been claiming repeatedly throughout the nearly-nine months of war so far; that the US has “decimated” Iran’s long-range fighting capability.

Both the US and Israel had also stated the goal of destroying Iran’s ballistic-missile capabilities when they launched war on 28 February.

Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza refugee camp

Hamas has confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, commander of the group’s Rafah Brigade, in an Israeli airstrike on a Gaza refugee camp on Saturday night.

The Israeli military said it had taken steps to “mitigate harm to civilians” in the strike. It said it had also targeted other Hamas militants in the strike but gave no further detail.

Israel’s military first announced the killing on Sunday, saying they had targeted Younis who they said had been working on restoring Hamas and getting members to “advance and carry out terror attacks”.

Younis had been one of the senior Hamas figures who helped plan and oversee the October 7 attacks. He had only been the Rafah brigade leader role for two months, after Israel killed his predecessor, Nael Abu Obeid.

In their statement announcing his death, Hamas said Younis was “one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack”.

Earlier this week, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital, the largest operational hospital in southern Gaza, killed at least six people, including a surgeon and patients, and injured 30, local officials said. The IDF said it had been targeting a commander of Hamas’s armed wing.

Israel is still striking Gaza on a near daily basis despite the the US-brokered ceasefire having come into action since October last year. More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, and more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza since the war began.

Here’s a recap of what the various sides have said this morning regarding the latest Iranian strikes targeting a US air base in Bahrain.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards:

The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force.

The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry

Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain.

[Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.

I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all American military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack. Those strikes also targeted a radar site.

Bahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'

After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.

Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.

It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.

Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:

I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.

Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.

Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.

They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.

US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.

Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.

The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.

That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.

Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.

Iran has targeted an airbase inBahrainin the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.

According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.

Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.

Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.

There are fears Iran’s attacks this morning might signal a resumption of the war while US President Donald Trump has threatened but refrained from returning to major combat. Negotiations to end the war remain at a stalemate, with the US maintaining its naval blockade and Iran its stranglehold over the strait of Hormuz.

Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.

The Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia, fighting the Houthis, have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, giving the Iran-aligned rebels even greater control over the critical shipping lane, which Saudi Arabia and other Gulf oil producers had been relying on to get their supplies out.

Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.

articles.title: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course on Sunday
articles.summary: The temporary order is part of a months-long challenge to the US president's plans to upgrade East Potomac Golf Links into a championship course.
articles.preview: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations. Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.
articles.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".

"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

Her order will last until 28 November.

A coalition of advocacy and legal groups opposing the closure and renovation said they are "grateful that the court has stopped the government from unlawfully closing East Potomac Park and depriving people of this priceless piece of American history and wonderful recreation space".

"Our laws prevent this administration from acting without a fair and public process, and today's order will stop the government from ignoring those laws," said the coalition, which represents the plaintiffs and includes Democracy Forward and the Democracy Defenders Fund. "We are eager to continue to argue this case in court."

The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.

The historic course, which sits two miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service (NPS) in the nation's capital.

The legal fight then escalated in October when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.

After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate for the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post on Truth Social.

Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether justice department attorneys had "made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".

That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans had been "done in bad faith", and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.

She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

articles.title: Indonesia President Prabowo apologises to Singapore, Malaysia over transboundary haze
articles.summary: According to a statement from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat, Prabowo also said 16 firefighters had died and two helicopters were lost battling forest fires that had raged for nearly four months.
articles.preview: According to a statement from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat, Prabowo also said 16 firefighters had died and two helicopters were lost battling forest fires that had raged for nearly four months. MANILA: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto apologised on Sunday (Nov 15) for the transboundary haze from forest and land fires in his country that has affected Singapore and Malaysia, according to a statement from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat.
articles.body:
According to a statement from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat, Prabowo also said 16 firefighters had died and two helicopters were lost battling forest fires that had raged for nearly four months.

MANILA: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto apologised on Sunday (Nov 15) for the transboundary haze from forest and land fires in his country that has affected Singapore and Malaysia, according to a statement from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat.

The statement, issued late on Sunday following the first day of the 49th ASEAN Leaders' Summit in Manila, said Prabowo had conveyed the apology on behalf of the Indonesian government and people while assuring regional leaders that his country had done its utmost to tackle the fires.

The fires, which persisted for nearly four months, have caused transboundary haze affecting communities in Singapore and Malaysia, the statement said.

Prabowo said his government maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corporations involved in forest fires and that various law enforcement measures have been taken, including the revocation of concessions and the initiation of legal proceedings against companies suspected of being responsible.

"We have revoked 17 corporate concessions. Twenty-six companies are currently under investigation, and 11 have been charged,” said Prabowo.

“Another 23 companies are slated to be charged. In total, 104 companies are under investigation by our police force."

Addressing the leaders of ASEAN member states, Prabowo said that Indonesia has made significant efforts to control the forest fires.

He said the Indonesian government has deployed 71,000 personnel, with 16 firefighters losing their lives and many others sustaining injuries during firefighting operations.

Two helicopters were also lost, he said.

Prabowo also stressed the need to shift Indonesia's approach to forest and land fires from firefighting and mitigation towards systematic prevention, according to the statement.

Indonesia is preparing to establish a new agency and implement various programs to strengthen future prevention of forest and land fires, he said.

SINGAPORE-INDONESIA COOPERATION

The apology comes after Singapore and Indonesia agreed last month to establish a joint task force to investigate companies linked to forest and land fires behind the transboundary haze.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also proposed on Sunday that the task force be expanded into an ASEAN-wide platform for sharing information and evidence, to help countries hold companies accountable for haze-causing fires.

articles.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
articles.preview: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
articles.body:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: ASEAN, China reach provisional agreement on 80% of South China Sea code, says Philippines
articles.summary: Negotiations on the long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct remain unfinished despite substantial progress, as ASEAN leaders also discuss Myanmar's political crisis and transboundary haze.
articles.preview: Negotiations on the long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct remain unfinished despite substantial progress, as ASEAN leaders also discuss Myanmar's political crisis and transboundary haze. MANILA: ASEAN and China have reached provisional agreement on about 80 per cent of the negotiating text for a long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct, Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said on Sunday (Nov 15).
articles.body:
Negotiations on the long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct remain unfinished despite substantial progress, as ASEAN leaders also discuss Myanmar's political crisis and transboundary haze.

MANILA: ASEAN and China have reached provisional agreement on about 80 per cent of the negotiating text for a long-awaited South China Sea Code of Conduct, Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said on Sunday (Nov 15).

Speaking at a press conference after the first day of the 49th ASEAN Leaders' Summit in Manila, Lazaro said the parties had agreed to continue working constructively to conclude negotiations on an effective and substantive code as soon as possible.

“Definitely, there is no conclusion yet," Lazaro told reporters.

Lazaro said differing positions among ASEAN member states and China, as well as the time needed for negotiations, had prevented the agreement from being finalised this year.

"If we were given probably another five to six months, we can finish that," she said.

The Philippines, which holds ASEAN's rotating chairmanship this year, had made concluding the negotiations by the end of 2026 a key priority.

Lazaro noted that the Philippines had made substantial progress, raising the proportion of agreed text from about 50 per cent to 80 per cent.

Singapore takes over the bloc's chairmanship in 2027, and Lazaro expressed confidence that negotiations could be concluded next year.

“I trust that Singapore will be able to finish the discussions,” she said.

The Code of Conduct is intended to establish rules to manage tensions in the disputed South China Sea, where Beijing's expansive maritime claims overlap with those of several Southeast Asian nations.

The Philippines and China have repeatedly clashed in the waterway, one of the world’s major shipping routes.

Other ASEAN countries, namely Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei, also have overlapping claims with China. While Indonesia is not a claimant state, its North Natuna waters, which lie on the edge of the South China Sea, have also seen clashes between the Indonesian coast guard and Chinese fishing boats.

Lazaro said negotiators had reached a provisional agreement on how the existing 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) relates to the proposed Code of Conduct.

Under the agreement, the declaration would provide the foundation for the new code, which would establish more substantive provisions to guide the conduct of parties in the waterway.

The parties also agreed that the code would serve as a platform for practical maritime cooperation and a mechanism to manage differences at sea, rather than settle competing territorial claims, Lazaro said.

The Philippines oversaw nine rounds of negotiations and two senior officials' meetings this year, with Malaysia and China co-chairing the Code of Conduct negotiations.

MYANMAR'S POLITICAL REPRESENTATION

ASEAN leaders also agreed to pursue calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased, progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground, Lazaro said.

This is subject to sustained, concrete progress in implementing the bloc's Five-Point Consensus, and ASEAN may consider gradually restoring Myanmar’s full political representation, she added.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said earlier in the day that the groups’ leaders had agreed to continue "constructive and principled engagement" with Myanmar while staying true to the principles of the Five-Point Consensus.

“But we need to ask ourselves, what more can we do for Myanmar? Ultimately, the crisis in Myanmar is about people, families who have been displaced, communities that need humanitarian assistance, and young people whose future has been interrupted by conflict and instability,” said Marcos.

Lazaro said at the press conference later in the day that ASEAN leaders had agreed on a "calibrated engagement, step-by-step and progress-based approach" to restoring Myanmar's participation.

The Five-Point Consensus, agreed in April 2021 following the military coup in Myanmar in February 2021, calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among all parties, the delivery of humanitarian assistance and a special envoy of the ASEAN chair to facilitate mediation of the dialogues. Lazaro is the current special envoy.

ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus

Following a 2021 military coup, ASEAN has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.

During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar.

The five points are:

First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint.

Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people.

Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN.

Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre.

Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.

She said ASEAN would monitor Myanmar's progress, particularly in ending hostilities, before considering restoring political representation.

"We want to see how Myanmar responds to that, because right now there are still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people," she said.

Myanmar's military leadership has been excluded from ASEAN's high-level meetings since 2021 for failing to implement the peace plan.

A director-general responsible for ASEAN affairs, rather than a political representative, represented the country at Sunday's summit.

Lazaro said Myanmar's representative outlined steps the country had taken, but other ASEAN members believed more was needed before its foreign minister could return to formal meetings.

TRANSBOUNDARY HAZE

Lazaro said ASEAN leaders also called for stronger action against companies and individuals responsible for forest fires contributing to transboundary haze that affected Singapore, parts of Malaysia, Brunei and the Philippines.

Indonesia had been frank and candid about the efforts it has undertaken to tackle forest fires within its borders, said Lazaro, without revealing details.

She said the leaders also encouraged ASEAN member states to prioritise ratifying the agreement establishing the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control.

The proposed centre, to be based in Indonesia, is intended to strengthen regional coordination in monitoring, preventing, and responding to transboundary haze.

ASEAN has sought to address the problem through its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, which entered into force in 2003.

The ASEAN Leaders’ Summit will continue until Tuesday, as the bloc holds separate summits with partners such as China, India and Japan.

China’s Premier Li Qiang is scheduled to attend the summit, and US President Donald Trump will attend an ASEAN-US summit on Tuesday evening.

articles.body:
Cambodia

The 20th Francophonie Summit opened in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on Sunday bringing together heads of state, government leaders, and high-level delegations from more than 80 French-speaking territories.

But the two-days of talks are being overshadowed by tensions between Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Rwanda over their candidates to be the organisation's new head.

The International Organisation of the Francophonie is set to elect its next secretary-general on Monday for a four-year term.

Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo has led the organisation for eight years and is running for a third term, but Kinshasa is strongly opposed to this and has threatened to quit if she is re-elected.

Kinshasa has proposed Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of national hero Patrice Lumumba, but said Saturday it could withdraw her candidacy if Rwanda did likewise.

There are tensions between the neighbouring countries over the ongoing conflict in the eastern DRC, with Kinshasa accusing Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group's activities in the region, which Kigali denies.

Rwanda earlier this week denounced Paris's involvement in the election of a new secretary general.

It said that French President Emmanuel Macron asked his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, to withdraw its candidate - a request Kigali said it had rejected.

France had supported Mushikiwabo in 2018 as ties warmed between Paris and Kigali, but had publicly expressed neutrality in this year's contest.

After news of Macron's efforts emerged, his office on Saturday said Paris had suggested both the Congolese and Rwandan candidates withdraw in the interests of unity.

In his opening address, Macron warned against "internal fractures" saying the organisation should "ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength - namely, its unity".

“Our shared language calls on us to engage in dialogue and mediation. It strengthens our ability to bring peoples together and to find jointly agreed solutions. It gives us the words and the tools to ensure that law prevails over force," he said.

The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), a post-colonial entity resembling the Commonwealth, gathers around 90 states and nations including 53 full members.

Last year Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF after successive coups that saw Paris-friendly governments replaced by pro-Russian juntas.

The departure of DR Congo - the second most Francophone country after France with 57.3 million speakers, according to the OIF - would be a major blow.

articles.title: Can Netanyahu and Eisenkot form a ‘unity’ government in Israel?
articles.summary: Yashar and Likud are scheduled to hold talks on Sunday, but will need to overcome major differences to work together.

Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his appeal for a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, casting a coalition that would keep him in power as integral to Israel’s national security. In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said his meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”.
articles.body:
Likud and Yashar, their parties, are scheduled to hold talks on Sunday, but will need to overcome major differences to work together.

Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his appeal for a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, casting a coalition that would keep him in power as integral to Israel’s national security.

In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said his meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”. He said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all” and claimed Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party and the man given the first shot to form Israel’s next government by President Isaac Herzog, called Netanyahu’s appeal a “bluff”.

“Nice try, but these tricks don’t work on me. Nor on Israel’s citizens,” Eisenkot said.

But Eisenkot confirmed that Yashar and Netanyahu’s Likud Party were talking about the proposal for a shared government.

So what, if anything, would it take for them to govern together, and what other options does Eisenkot have?

How do the numbers in the Knesset add up?

In Israel’s October 27 election, the four-party bloc led by Eisenkot won 48 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53. Two Palestinian-led factions, the Joint List and Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List, won a record 19 seats between them.

Last week, Eisenkot’s bloc showed what it could do with the backing of both Palestinian-led factions, securing a 63-to-50 vote to approve the makeup of the Arrangements Committee, a panel that helps set the Knesset’s agenda while coalition talks are under way. The bloc then moved to set up temporary committees overseeing finance, foreign affairs and defence.

Eisenkot’s bloc and the two Arab-led factions hold 67 seats combined, six more than needed for an outright majority. Another possibility is a minority government backed by Ra’am’s eight lawmakers. Their support would give Eisenkot 56 votes against Netanyahu’s 53 if the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers abstained or stayed away from the confidence vote. That would allow a government to take office with fewer than 61 votes in favour, but it would depend on how all three groups voted.

But getting Eisenkot’s allies to agree to such a deal is another matter. Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats, is open to working with the Palestinian-led factions, while Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman and Together leader Naftali Bennett have rejected a coalition with Palestinians. However, both served in the government formed in 2021, when Ra’am became the first Arab party to formally join an Israeli governing coalition.

“One of Eisenkot’s main difficulties is the opposition of Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett [leaders of parties in his alliance] to relying on Arab parties,” Yasser Manna, a researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Studies on Israeli Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “This position restricts Eisenkot’s coalition options, but it does not automatically make a unity government with Netanyahu more likely. Instead, it increases the importance of negotiations with other parties, particularly the ultra-Orthodox parties.”

The other main option, which according to experts is the most likely scenario, is the Eisenkot bloc going into a coalition with both ultra-Orthodox parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which would take the Eisenkot bloc to 61.

Advisers from one faction of United Torah Judaism have reportedly sought a written commitment from all 48 lawmakers in Eisenkot’s bloc to pass a law exempting Jewish religious seminary students from military service and to shield it from being struck down by the High Court. Eisenkot and Lieberman are reportedly opposed to this compromise.

Could Eisenkot and Netanyahu govern together?

President Herzog gave Eisenkot until December 6 to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days, which would take the deadline to December 20.

Eisenkot has left the door open to members of Netanyahu’s Likud Party and to far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, provided they back a government led by Eisenkot and accept his programme.

“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said at the ceremony where Herzog handed him the mandate.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that agreeing to meet can serve both men politically. “The coalition formation period is about spin and distortion and trying to gain leverage,” he told Al Jazeera. “So you take a meeting to show that you were willing to talk, then say the other side made unreasonable demands.”

The two men know each other well. Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and served as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet during the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. He left the emergency government in June 2024.

“I believe the relationship between Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot is marked by a deep crisis of trust that goes beyond political competition,” Manna said. “However, it is important to distinguish between their political disagreements and their relatively similar approaches to national security. Both prioritise military and security considerations, particularly regarding the Palestinians and Iran.”

An early test could come on Tuesday, when Eisenkot’s allies plan to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Likud with Yashar lawmaker Matan Kahana. Eisenkot has challenged Netanyahu and Smotrich to back Kahana and allow the vote to go ahead as scheduled, saying their response would show how serious they are about cooperation.

But even if Eisenkot and Netanyahu agreed on a policy plan for government, they still have to decide who leads. “The question of who would serve as prime minister remains the central obstacle,” Manna said. “Eisenkot has so far rejected a rotation arrangement with Netanyahu.”

Could a security crisis change the talks?

Meanwhile, Netanyahu is still in office as caretaker prime minister while negotiations continue. That gives him an incentive to exploit divisions among Eisenkot’s potential partners and wait for his mandate to run out, experts say.

“At this stage, Netanyahu does not necessarily need to form a new coalition himself,” Manna said. “Preventing Eisenkot from forming one may be enough to preserve his position temporarily.”

Manna said Netanyahu could also use a security crisis to increase pressure for a national government. “A renewed large-scale confrontation could increase pressure for a national unity government or shift the priorities of coalition negotiations,” he said. “At the same time, it could generate new disagreements over military decision-making, the management of the conflict, and the authority of a caretaker government.”

If talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties fail, Levy said, Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between accepting support from the Palestinian-led parties and leaving Netanyahu in office. He could also propose a short-lived government whose immediate purpose would be to replace Netanyahu and prepare for another election.

He added that in such a scenario, Eisenkot might tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

This would prevent Netanyahu from using “his position as prime minister to create a crisis”.

articles.body:
Singapore – Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, under scrutiny for allegedly steering Nvidia chips to China, said on Sunday that suspected spy Alice Huang had left the firm more than a year ago.

Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese firms get around U.S. export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China.

Its former director, Alice Huang, has been identified in U.S. media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned as the tech giant’s chief executive on Thursday.

“Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” the firm said.

“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters.”

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related. Beijing has denied the spying allegations.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a Nov. 8 letter to Nvidia employees that did not name the woman involved. He resigned days later.

Nvidia’s board has said it will investigate the matter, and three U.S. Congress committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18.

Megaspeed said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business“, and that it was aware of media reports “containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence“.

The tech group also said it has retained an external legal counsel “to conduct a thorough internal investigation” of its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws, which limit the transfer of some advanced chips to China.

Singapore authorities said servers containing advanced AI chips were being exported to Malaysia and were suspected of being delivered to other destinations, contrary to declarations made in the city-state.

Investigations into Megaspeed “are ongoing“, Singapore’s police force has said.

Authorities also said they had barred Alice Huang in February from re-entering the city-state after she provided inaccurate information during a probe into Megaspeed.

She was not, however, investigated for espionage.

articles.summary: Did Trump's Pakistan pivot cost him support in the US midterms? Submitted by Ali Jaswal on Sun, 11/15/2026 - 11:01 Pakistani Americans who backed Trump in 2024 say they switched to the Democrats after the US president abandoned Imran Khan and embraced Pakistan’s military leadership Supporters celebrate at a midterm election night watch party for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on 4 November 2026 (Salwan Georges/Getty Images via AFP) Off Several Pakistani Americans who helped Donald Trump return to the White House in 2024 have told Middle East Eye that the diaspora community turned against him in last week's midterm elections after the US president "abandoned" his promise to secure the release of Pakistan's imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. They said their disillusionment deepened as Trump cultivated a close relationship with Pakistan's powerful army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, whom he has repeatedly called his "favourite field marshal". While the US does not release official demographic breakdowns of voting patterns, an estimated 680,000 people of Pakistani origin lived in the country in 2023, according to the Pew Research Center. Although they represent a relatively small share of the electorate, concentrated communities in politically competitive states such as Michigan and Pennsylvania give them potentially significant influence. Syed Ali, a corporate finance professional living in Virginia's Eighth Congressional District, told MEE that he threw his support behind Democratic candidates and "voted for anybody that was non-Republican". Ali, who voted for Republican candidates in 2024, said that before Trump entered office, there was a feeling of hope that the US president "was going to do something to restore democracy in Pakistan and [call] for the release of Imran Khan". He suggested that the US deliberately supported the imprisonment of Khan, as this helped them get rid of a prominent voice on Palestine and Iran. "Khan would have created a ruckus with whatever was happening with the genocide, and of course he would have played a key role in the Iran war. He was the loudest voice for Palestine, so purposely he was kept in jail," Ali added. Khan's imprisonment has become a rallying point for much of the Pakistani diaspora in the US. The former prime minister had accused the Biden administration of orchestrating a "regime change operation" against his government in 2022, in collusion with Pakistan's military and opposition parties. 'The reason I voted for Trump was because of him, and the reason I voted for Democrats is because of him' - Naveen Sheikh, Virginia resident The Biden administration's subsequent support for Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif drove many in the diaspora towards Trump and Republicans in 2024. But that support has since unravelled. Major Pakistani American organisations, including the Pakistani-American Public Affairs Committee (PAKPAC USA), First Pakistan Global (FPG) and the Community Alliance for Peace and Justice (CAPJ), backed Democratic candidates in the midterms through public events, advocacy and fundraising. Nearly all had previously rallied behind Trump. The shift has been fuelled by military operations in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir, deteriorating human rights conditions in Pakistan, military interventions in Afghanistan as well as Khan's prolonged imprisonment. "The reason I voted for Trump was because of him, and the reason I voted for Democrats is because of him, and also the two unwanted wars and the rise in oil prices," Naveen Sheikh, a management professional in Virginia's 11th Congressional District, told MEE. Sheikh voted for Democratic candidate James Walkinshaw but did not vote for Senator-elect Mark Warner. "Because we have been approaching him about Imran Khan, and we have had high-level meetings, but no outcome. He was like, whatever," she added. Trump's 'favourite field marshal' After Trump's 2024 election victory, prominent figures in his political circle, including special envoy Richard Grenell and Republican Congressman Joe Wilson, publicly voiced support for Khan's release and criticised Munir, Pakistan's army chief. But relations shifted following last year's confrontation between India and Pakistan, when Munir forged a close relationship with Trump, including a visit to the White House. For many Pakistani Americans, the relationship came to symbolise the administration's abandonment of its earlier promises. Pakistan's new clout puts it at centre of fragile geopolitical web  Joe Wilson last year, who is a staunch national security Republican, turned out a tactic to pressure the Pakistani regime to do exactly what Trump wanted them to do," Mehlaqa Samdhani, a founding member of CAPJ, told MEE. "So people just felt quite disillusioned and betrayed by Republicans." Introduced in early 2025, the proposed legislation called for sanctions against members of Pakistan's leadership, including Munir, over human rights violations and Khan's imprisonment. The relevant House committees never considered it. Republicans on the House Committee on Rules also voted in September last year to block two proposed amendments to the National Defence Authorization Act that sought to make US military assistance to Pakistan conditional on human rights improvements. Democrats backed the measures. Pakistani American organisations subsequently began engaging more actively with Democratic candidates, seeking commitments on future US policy towards Islamabad. 'Pakistan policy is mainly formulated by US Central Command and the Central Intelligence Agency, and to some extent by the State Department. It is not easy to turn it around overnight' - Zoobia Chaudhry, First Pakistan Global Some also began calling for congressional investigations into alleged corrupt dealings involving Pakistan's military leadership, Trump's family and close associates - particularly over mineral and cryptocurrency agreements. But activists acknowledge that changing Washington's Pakistan policy will not be straightforward. "Pakistan policy is mainly formulated by US Central Command and the Central Intelligence Agency, and to some extent by the State Department," Zoobia Chaudhry, a physician and communications director at FPG, told MEE. "It is not easy to turn it around overnight." She said the organisation's immediate priority would be to push for "investigations and sanctions in the new Congress" against Munir and other senior figures in Pakistan's leadership. Backlash beyond the Pakistani diaspora The backlash has also crossed ideological lines within the Pakistani American community. Some conservative Muslims who had voted Republican for decades because of shared social values chose Democrats despite their opposition to progressive policies, particularly those concerning LGBTQ+ and transgender issues in schools and public life. Trump's campaign rhetoric targeting Muslims further deepened their disillusionment. "The bottom line is they will continue voting with the left because of the massive bigotry, xenophobia and Islamophobia from the right," Junaid Khan, president of PAKPAC's DC, Maryland and Virginia chapter, told MEE. "I don't see this community coming back to the GOP anytime soon. It's an attack on identity. It went too far." How Pakistan positioned itself at the centre of global crisis management  by Khan's struggle for democracy and the rule of law, is now considering joining the Democratic Party. PAKPAC, one of the largest political action committees representing Pakistani Americans, endorsed several Democratic candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, but none of the Republicans. Its support for Trump in 2024 had surprised many. The discontent has also extended beyond Pakistani Americans, with Trump's approach to Khan and Pakistan's military leadership drawing criticism among other South Asian and Muslim communities in the US. Hussain Nadim, a former research fellow at the United States Institute of Peace and the Wilson Center, said the communities were interconnected rather than politically isolated. He noted that one of the largest protests for Khan in Silicon Valley had been organised by Indians, for whom the former prime minister is also a cricketing hero. They were also angered by Trump's apparent endorsement of Pakistan's military leadership and what they saw as his willingness to undermine democracy in a developing country. "So this issue added to a broader wave within these communities who felt betrayed by the Trump administration," Nadim said. articles.summary: The elections commission says this will allow for the implementation of additional processes including distribution of registration materials and civic education.

Initially scheduled for 2015, the authorities have postponed the elections several times before and repeatedly extended the transitional period.
articles.body:
South Sudan

People in South Sudan began registering to vote on Saturday as the country postponed its first general elections since independence from Sudan in 2011.

The National Elections Commission said the polls, due to take place in December, have been moved to 11 February.

Initially scheduled for 2015, the authorities have postponed the elections several times before and repeatedly extended the transitional period.

"The commission would like to take the opportunity to make it clear that the adjustment of the electoral timeline should not be misconstrued as a discussion to abandon or to call off the elections,” said Commission spokesperson, Josephine Achiro.

She said the extension would allow for the implementation of additional processes including distribution of registration materials and civic education.

Saturday’s announcement came amid growing violence, political battles between the country’s president and deposed vice president, and slow voter registration.

There have been concerns from regional and international partners over the country’s readiness to hold credible elections in December.

Former vice-president Riek Machar, President Salva Kiir’s main opponent, has been under house arrest since March 2025, accused of "crimes against humanity".

A bloody civil war between the forces of the two men between 2013 and 2018 led to more than 400,000 deaths.

A 2018 peace accord brought in a government of national unity with Kiir as president and Machar his deputy, their joint administration tasked with paving the way to elections in 2022.

Those elections, however, have been repeatedly postponed and the administration has implemented virtually none of the provisions in the peace agreement.

Machar was suspended and charged with treason and murder in 2025.

The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan recently warned a December election could set off widespread conflict if used to dismantle the 2018 accord.

Gabriel Bol Deng Majok, chairperson of the National Elections Commission appealed to politicians to refrain from using violence telling them to speak “to the mind, heart, and soul” of the people.

“If you want to be the leader that our citizens want, it will happen. But not through violence, not through bullets, only through ballot papers," he said.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned about conditions in the country, including the displacement of tens of thousands of people and the disruption of international humanitarian operations.

In addition, the World Bank estimates that some 90 per cent of South Sudan's 15 million inhabitants having no state-recognised identification, complicating voter registration and presenting significant logistical challenges for a December vote.

Authorities have set up more than 3,100 registration centres across the country, a process theoretically due to last two weeks, but officials said not all the necessary equipment was in place.
