Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi plans to propose at an upcoming regional summit in Manila the creation of an Asian version of the International Energy Agency (IEA), informed sources said Sunday.

Through the envisioned framework, which would call for cooperation in oil stockpiling in preparation for energy crises, Japan aims to strengthen Asia’s energy supply chains, whose vulnerability has been exposed in the wake of the ongoing Middle East turmoil.

Takaichi will present the plan at a summit Tuesday of the 11-member Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), a regional cooperation framework for realizing carbon neutrality, the sources said.

Japan will play a role in establishing the Asian version of the IEA while the Jakarta-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, or ERIA, which investigates and researches energy security issues in the region, will serve as the secretariat for the new framework.

Working with the Paris-based IEA’s new base to be set up in Tokyo, the new regional framework will help member nations share expertise on oil stockpiling and make rules on the release and sharing of oil reserves in the event of an emergency.

The IEA, established in 1974, after the first oil crisis, requires member countries to stockpile oil equivalent to 90 days of consumption.

In response to the Middle East tensions, IEA member countries jointly released oil reserves on a large scale in and after March this year. But no ASEAN member nations participated in the concerted initiative.

In April, Japan, which relies on ASEAN countries for the supply of oil-based products such as surgical gloves, announced the launch of the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia, or Powerr Asia, which is designed to help make the region’s supply chains resilient.

Elsewhere at the AZEC summit, Takaichi is expected to propose the use of idled oil storage tanks in Japan. Specifically, Japan will consider cooperating for a Philippines-led initiative to develop a joint oil reserve system for Southeast Asia and establishing a mechanism allowing nations in the region to buy oil on a priority base in the event of an emergency.

The AZEC members other than Japan and the Philippines are Australia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

articles.title: Melaka result bolsters Malay political alliance, posing tougher challenge for Malaysia PM Anwar ahead of GE
articles.summary: The landslide victory showcased how a BN-PN alliance could achieve success at the next Malaysian general election, while dealing a blow to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan and its tentative efforts to forge an electoral understanding with Muhyiddin Yassin’s Bersatu.
articles.preview: The landslide victory showcased how a BN-PN alliance could achieve success at the next Malaysian general election, while dealing a blow to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan and its tentative efforts to forge an electoral understanding with Muhyiddin Yassin’s Bersatu.
articles.body:
analysis Asia

The landslide victory showcased how a BN-PN alliance could achieve success at the next Malaysian general election, while dealing a blow to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan and its tentative efforts to forge an electoral understanding with Muhyiddin Yassin’s Bersatu.

MELAKA: The commanding victory of the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional (BN-PN) alliance in the Melaka state election has highlighted its strong appeal among Malay voters and pointed the way to possible success at Malaysia’s next general election.

But beyond the landslide victory, the results also point to an increasingly polarised electorate, with the Malay-Muslim unity narrative championed by the UMNO and PAS parties not only consolidating Malay support behind BN-PN but also appearing to drive non-Malay ethnic minority voters towards the Democratic Action Party (DAP).

Analysts say the contrasting voting patterns could further entrench Malaysia’s ethnic political divide ahead of the next general election, the country’s sixteenth (GE16), creating a particularly difficult challenge for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, which relies on a multiracial support base.

Although Melaka accounts for only a small fraction of Malaysia's parliamentary constituencies, the result offers another test of a new electoral alliance that has already delivered victories in neighbouring states.

BN and PN swept 24 of the 28 seats in the Melaka state assembly in Saturday’s (Nov 14) polls, with BN winning 21 and PN securing three, while PH retained just four seats, all won by DAP.

BN and PH are allies in Anwar’s federal government, but the two coalitions have clashed in recent state polls following the former’s decision to work with PN under a Malay unity pact.

The arrangement reflects Malaysia's increasingly fluid coalition politics: BN helps keep Anwar's government in power nationally, but it has joined forces with the opposition PN in state elections, putting it in direct competition with the prime minister's own PH coalition.

Political analyst James Chin said the result exemplified a growing wave of support by the Malay community for BN-PN.

Although the combined BN-PN tally represents a gain of only one seat from the 2021 election, when the two coalitions contested separately, larger winning margins in many Malay-majority constituencies suggest their electoral cooperation has paid dividends.

The results, which largely matched pollsters’ predictions, underscore the effectiveness of the pact in consolidating Malay votes and avoiding the three-cornered contests that had previously benefited PH.

The Malay-Muslim unity campaign seeks to bring together parties that have historically competed for the support of Malaysia's ethnic Malay majority, most of whom are Muslim. Supporters argue that political cooperation would strengthen Malay-Muslim representation, while critics fear it could deepen ethnic and religious divisions.

However, the outcome presents a paradox: The same Malay-Muslim unity campaign that has strengthened BN-PN’s hold over Malay voters also appears to have reinforced non-Malay support for DAP, leaving Anwar’s Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) and Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) increasingly squeezed.

The failure of PKR and Amanah to capture a single seat highlights the coalition’s difficulty in appealing to Malay voters, while the complete rout of former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin’s Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) raises questions over whether its tentative cooperation with PH can offer any meaningful electoral advantage.

Political analysts said that the Melaka results could intensify pressure on Anwar to call an early general election, although the prime minister has every incentive to delay the polls and allow BN-PN’s momentum to dissipate. GE16 must be called by February 2028.

Azmi Hassan, who is senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, told CNA: “It will be some time yet before GE16. Even though BN and PN will want it to be held as soon as possible to bank on their momentum, the final word (on when) will be the prime minister’s.”

The prime minister “will hold the fort for as long as he can as PH is in a weak position,” he added.

BLUE WAVE ‘UNBEATABLE’ IN MALAY-MAJORITY SEATS

The analyst Chin said the outcome in Melaka was widely anticipated, describing the Malay electoral wave as further evidence of the formidable strength of the BN-PN partnership.

Chin said the results demonstrated that votes were largely transferable between the two coalitions, with supporters for BN and PN likely casting ballots for each other’s candidates, making their electoral cooperation a potent weapon against PH.

“They are unbeatable as a combo,” added Chin, who is Professor of Asian Studies at the University of Tasmania and Senior Research Associate at Malaysia’s Tun Tan Cheng Lock Institute of Social Studies.

The Election Commission reported a voter turnout of 71.77 per cent, with political analyst Azmi attributing the relatively strong participation largely to Malay voters energised by the campaign’s emphasis on Malay-Muslim unity. The 2021 state polls saw an overall turnout of 65.85 per cent.

According to data estimates released by ElectionData.MY, 78.1 per cent of the Malays came out to vote, while only 58.8 per cent of the Chinese and 58 per cent of the Indian community cast their ballots. For the 2021 polls, Malay turnout was 72.3 per cent, as published by Malaysia Dateline.

Azmi said the mobilisation of Malay voters, compared with what he assessed to be weaker participation among non-Malays, was a key factor in the alliance’s victory.

“The Malays came out in droves … and that made a difference,” he told CNA.

The strength of the so-called “blue wave” was particularly evident in UMNO’s traditional rural strongholds, where several prominent leaders secured comfortable victories. Blue refers to the signature colours of both BN and PN flags.

Melaka Chief Minister Ab Rauf Yusoh retained his Tanjung Bidara seat with an 8,615-vote majority, a dramatic increase from his razor-thin 364-vote majority in 2021.

UMNO’s firebrand youth chief Muhamad Akmal Saleh won Merlimau by 8,724 votes, while the popular Mohd Noor Helmy Abdul Halem secured Duyong with a majority of 10,040 votes, having clinched the seat by just 200 votes in 2021.

The alliance also demonstrated its strength in more ethnically mixed constituencies, with BN’s MCA candidate Lim Ban Hong winning Kelebang by 7,035 votes. Lim won by just 876 seats in 2021.

Perhaps the most significant casualty was Amanah vice-president and former Melaka chief minister Adly Zahari, who lost Bukit Katil to PAS candidate Mohd Ridzuan Sarif by 6,607 votes.

His defeat was particularly telling given that Adly was among PH’s most recognisable Malay leaders in the state and that PM Anwar himself had campaigned for him on the ground on at least two occasions.

Chin predicted that for the upcoming General Election, the BN-PN alliance could apply the same formula, and easily sweep Malay-majority constituencies in Peninsular Malaysia and secure between 100 and 105 parliamentary seats at GE16, putting it within striking distance of the 112 seats needed for a simple majority.

Such a result would leave the pact well-positioned to seek the backing of parties from Sabah and Sarawak to form the next federal government.

But analysts cautioned that the alliance’s greatest challenge will be when negotiations between UMNO and PAS begin over who should contest parliamentary seats in Malay heartland areas where the latter have been dominant.

Syaza Shukri, a political scientist at the International Islamic University Malaysia, said the Malay community remained enthusiastic about penyatuan ummah, or the Muslim unity agenda, which could sustain support for the pact even if GE16 is held late next year.

“(The) main concern is when it comes to seat negotiations. Yes, the people are happy to vote for them, but can the leaders agree to an acceptable seat arrangement, especially in SG4?”

SG4 refers to the four PAS-led northern states of Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis, where negotiations could prove especially difficult as UMNO seeks to reassert its dominance within the partnership.

Azmi similarly pointed out that seat negotiations in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka state elections had been relatively straightforward because BN was clearly the stronger partner in those states.

But the dynamics would be markedly different in PAS strongholds, as well as states such as Pahang and Perak, where both parties have substantial political interests.

“A failure to reach an acceptable compromise could threaten the alliance’s cohesion and undermine the electoral gains it has made so far,” said Azmi.

PH RETAINS NON-MALAY SUPPORT BUT BERSATU OFFERS LITTLE HELP

For PH, the retention of four seats by DAP offers some consolation, suggesting that the coalition continues to command significant support among non-Malay voters despite successive electoral defeats.

DAP held Ayer Keroh, Kesidang, Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir, all of which are ethnic Chinese-majority seats, although its winning margins narrowed in some constituencies compared with 2021.

But analysts say DAP’s ability to retain its traditional strongholds also reflects a growing unease among Chinese voters over the Malay-Muslim unity agenda advanced by BN-PN.

Political analyst Oh Ei Sun of the Singapore Institute of International Affairs said concerns over the campaign’s emphasis on Malay unity, particularly the prominent role played by Islamist party PAS, had likely encouraged Chinese voters to rally behind DAP.

“The grand Malay unity narrative has manifested excellently in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now Melaka. These are UMNO strongholds, but PAS is also now making their presence felt, gaining footholds in these states where previously they struggled in constituencies along the west coast of Peninsula Malaysia,” said Oh.

Oh further added that this presents a paradox for PH. While the Malay unity campaign may help DAP defend its strongholds by galvanising non-Malay voters, it simultaneously makes it harder for PKR and Amanah to win the Malay support needed to capture ethnically mixed constituencies.

He also warned that some ethnic minorities might instead choose to vote for Bersama or elect not to cast their vote.

“PKR and Amanah will struggle to gain any Malay votes in the upcoming election because the grand Malay narrative is taking hold …. It will lead to a more polarised Malaysia,” said Oh.

Syaza said she saw few effective options for PH to overcome the appeal of Malay-Muslim unity, even if Anwar were able to deliver on promised reforms and improve economic conditions.

“I don’t think it’s enough to counter the Malay unity agenda,” she said.

The poor performance of Bersatu has further complicated Anwar’s efforts to broaden PH’s appeal among Malay voters.

Despite informal cooperation that saw PH avoid contesting four constituencies where Bersatu fielded candidates, Muhyiddin’s party failed to win any of the seven seats it contested, losing its deposits in five after failing to garner enough votes.

Its strongest showing came in Pantai Kundor, where candidate Asmah Samat secured 6,112 votes against BN’s 8,864, but the party failed to make a meaningful impact elsewhere.

In Bemban, Bersatu managed just 2,109 votes, finishing behind Bersama, which garnered 4,140 votes, and PN’s victorious candidate, who secured 11,881 votes.

Azmi said Bersatu had failed to demonstrate that it could attract sufficient Malay support to become a “reliable electoral partner” for PH, casting doubt on the value of any future cooperation.

Syaza, however, offered a more measured assessment, saying Bersatu could still target constituencies in states such as Selangor if it developed a clearer political identity.

“Bersatu needs to figure out if they want to re-brand and aim for a wider pool of voters. This could work if it forms a pact with others, others its just splitting more votes and BN-PN will benefit,” she said.

For Bersama, meanwhile, another election without a single victory represents a setback to its ambitions of emerging as a credible alternative to established political parties.

The Rafizi-led party contested 16 seats but failed to win any, retaining its deposit only in Bemban, where it captured 22.5 per cent of valid votes.

Chin said Bersama had damaged its credibility by contesting in the Johor and Melaka state elections without securing a victory, arguing that it should have concentrated its resources on GE16.

“But they still have a chance because the core support of its leaders like Rafizi, Wong Chen and Lee Chean Chung is in the Klang Valley where they have established political bases,” he added.

WHAT’S NEXT FOR BN-PN, PH?

Attention will now turn to the timing of GE16, with BN-PN likely to seek an early election to capitalise on its string of victories in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka state elections.

But Anwar, whose government has been weakened politically by PH’s successive defeats, has little incentive to call a general election while the Malay unity wave remains strong.

Chin said the prime minister was likely to delay the polls for as long as possible, forcing BN and PN to maintain their uneasy partnership for another year or longer.

He added that the immediate electoral battleground will be Sarawak, which goes to the polls on Dec 12.

But Chin stressed that the political landscape there is markedly different, with the state dominated by Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS), and UMNO and PAS have limited presence. The contest is therefore unlikely to provide a comparable test of the BN-PN alliance’s strength.

For BN-PN, the coming months will instead be a test of whether it can preserve the momentum of its Malay unity campaign while resolving the potentially divisive question of seat allocations.

Complicating matters is BN’s continued participation in Anwar’s federal unity government, even as it strengthens its electoral cooperation with opposition bloc PN in preparation for the next general election.

Syaza told CNA that it is unlikely that BN would withdraw its support from Anwar to force an early election in the short term, as they have stopped short of doing this so far.

“GE might still have a long way to go, and BN-PN will use the time to negotiate seats and consolidate their alliance,” added Syaza.

“All the threats to pull support are just wayang (theatre),” she said.

articles.title: Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
articles.summary: Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could squeeze militias and avert internal strife
articles.preview: Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could financially squeeze militias and avert internal strife. The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad. The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.
articles.body:
Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could financially squeeze militias and avert internal strife.

The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.

The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.

At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.

For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.

That led Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to launch the crackdown, with an Iraqi security committee entering Jurf al-Nasr on Friday to investigate, following the arrest of other officials accused of graft. The formerly Sunni-majority area has long been considered outside government control since Iraqi militias seized the area a decade ago.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at Horizon Engage, told Al Jazeera that Jurf al-Sakhar’s value is deeply rooted in recent developments in Iraq, when Iran-linked militias used the campaign against ISIL (ISIS) to stamp their authority in the country.

“Iran-backed militias illegally seized and renamed Jurf al-Sakr when they conducted sectarian cleansing of the Sunni residents in the area in 2014, under the cover of the anti-Daesh [ISIL] war,” Knights explained.

The town, about 60km (37 miles) from Baghdad, is at a critical point near the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and Karbala.

It was once the site of Saddam Hussein’s military industrial complexes, which made Jurf al-Nasr an ideal place for Iraqi militias to test, build and hide rockets, drones and missiles, said Knights.

“If full control is taken, which is unlikely, the government would be able to finally tell Iraqis that a militia had been removed from its base and the legal residents of the area allowed to return,” he said. “This would be like taking back the Bekaa Valley from Hezbollah.”

Knights said the actual financial impact on Kataib Hezbollah of the Jurf al-Sakhar crackdown could be less spectacular than expected, with the militia having other sources of revenue.

Analysts say that dismantling the smuggling networks is part of a wider project to bring weapons under the control of the state.

After some Iran-linked militias missed a deadline to disarm this year, PM al-Zaidi now appears to be using economic pressure to weaken these armed groups without directly confronting them.

Security and strategic expert Saif Raad told Al Jazeera that the anticorruption campaign in Jurf al-Sakhar is essentially a message from the PM that no group is above the law.

“This duality is over. Part of what happened now is that the Iraqi people knew these factions and knew why they hold onto weapons, and I believe this is a victory achieved by the government without a single drop of Iraqi blood,” Raad said.

“Jurf al-Sakhar has been around for, let’s say, more than ten years; for ten years no prime minister was able to enter this area.”

Averting armed conflict

A central focus of the government’s strategy is executing this crackdown without igniting a potentially explosive ‘Shia-on-Shia’ armed conflict.

The militia network which emerged following the US-led invasion of Iraq – and was emboldened during the campaign against ISIL – includes groups with widely divergent political and religious views. Some are closely aligned to Iran and accused of being proxies of Tehran, while others are closer to the federal government.

In a bid to prevent violence, Al-Zaidi reportedly cooperated with leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), particularly with the Badr Organisation, before initiating the arrests and dismissals in Jurf al-Sakhar, Raad said.

Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that leveraging Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organisation, was essential to neutralising the threat from the militias.

“The Badr Organisation is considered the largest combat force within the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so the process of focusing on this issue… is a fundamental part of strengthening the state project,” Raad observed.

“[The campaign] is a major shift in the process of strengthening the state and state institutions and making the Popular Mobilisation Forces an active and large part in controlling these groups [militias outside government control].”

Political analyst Ali Fadhlallah said that due to the structural nature of Iraq’s political and religious leadership, an internal war between the Shia factions was never likely to break out, particularly due to the influence Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani.

“The Shia component has very many large and positive factors that serve as a brake for any clash that is supposed to happen,” Fadhlallah said.

“The presence of the rational religious authority, which has always controlled the rhythm of the political process at dangerous crossroads, definitely has a very large role and it is monitoring the events… the issue of a [Shia-Shia] clash is unlikely, even in the most difficult and miserable circumstances.”

articles.title: Teheran: 'Aiea troppo influenzata dagli Usa, perde credibilità'
articles.summary: Pasdaran rivendicano attacco a radar Usa in Bahrein con sei droni
articles.preview: Il portavoce del ministero degli Esteri iraniano ha criticato l'Agenzia internazionale per l'energia atomica (Aiea) per aver adottato un approccio parziale sotto l'influenza degli Stati Uniti, affermando che la condotta dell'Agenzia ne mina la credibilità e rende impossibile qualsiasi miglioramento delle relazioni con l'Iran nelle attuali circostanze. Lo scrive l'agenzia iraniana Tasnim.
articles.body:
Il portavoce del ministero degli Esteri iraniano ha criticato l'Agenzia internazionale per l'energia atomica (Aiea) per aver adottato un approccio parziale sotto l'influenza degli Stati Uniti, affermando che la condotta dell'Agenzia ne mina la credibilità e rende impossibile qualsiasi miglioramento delle relazioni con l'Iran nelle attuali circostanze. Lo scrive l'agenzia iraniana Tasnim.

Nel corso della conferenza stampa settimanale della domenica, Esmaeil Baghaei ha contestato un recente rapporto del dg dell'Aiea Rafael Grossi, sostenendo che l'Agenzia soffre di un problema strutturale nel modo in cui pubblica i propri documenti. Egli ha descritto tale criticità come una lacuna da colmare, aggiungendo che la sua persistenza appare intenzionale.

Baqaei ha affermato che l'Aiea, influenzata dagli Stati Uniti e dal loro approccio di parte, continua a insistere sulla linea d'azione intrapresa in precedenza. Ha inoltre avvertito che il rapporto, sbilanciato contro l'Iran, ha danneggiato la credibilità dell'Agenzia e comporterà delle responsabilità per quest'ultima. Baqaei ha rilevato che un aspetto significativo del rapporto di Grossi è il riconoscimento, da parte dell'Agenzia, del fatto che gli attacchi militari contro l'Iran hanno creato una situazione senza precedenti.

Tuttavia, ha osservato Baghaei, l'Aiea avrebbe dovuto dichiarare esplicitamente che l'aggressione militare da parte di Stati Uniti e Israele ne è stata la causa principale.

"Purtroppo, in seguito a tali attacchi, l'Aiea ha ignorato questo dato di fatto evidente", ha affermato. Baqaei ha ribadito che, finché persisterà l'attuale situazione, non sarà possibile alcun miglioramento nelle relazioni tra l'Iran e l'Agenzia.

Commentando la richiesta dell'Aiea di far rientrare i propri ispettori in Iran, Baghaei ha affermato che l'Agenzia non può avanzare una simile istanza senza tenere conto dei trascorsi della vicenda. "L'Aiea deve decidere se vuole essere un organismo tecnico o se intende rimanere sotto l'influenza di determinati Paesi", ha affermato.

L'Iran disporrebbe ancora di un arsenale compreso tra 1.500 e 2.500 missili, nonostante mesi di attacchi statunitensi e israeliani contro le sue infrastrutture militari. È quanto emerge da una valutazione dell'intelligence Usa citata dal Wall Street Journal, secondo cui Teheran manterrebbe capacità significative di colpire obiettivi statunitensi e alleati nella regione in caso di una ripresa della guerra. La stima è considerata a bassa affidabilità, precisano funzionari statunitensi, a causa delle difficoltà nel determinare quanti missili siano pronti al lancio e quanti siano custoditi nei depositi. La ricostituzione dell'arsenale iraniano è entrata nelle valutazioni dell'amministrazione Trump sull'eventualità di nuovi attacchi. Le valutazioni israeliane indicano a loro volta oltre 1.500 missili balistici ancora in possesso di Teheran.

"Chi è fuggito dalla propria abitazione per rifugiarsi in bunker militari, per paura delle minacce imminenti, farebbe meglio a riflettere sui propri fallimenti strategici nel Golfo Persico, invece di insultare le grandi nazioni", ha dichiarato il presidente del Parlamento iraniano Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, rivolgendosi al segretario al Tesoro statunitense Scott Bessent. Venerdì il funzionario statunitense aveva definito l'Iran un "animale pericoloso messo alle strette", dopo essere stato presumibilmente minacciato dal governo iraniano. Secondo quanto riferito, Bessent era stato costretto a trasferirsi dalla propria abitazione in una base militare. "Le dichiarazioni assurde e il linguaggio immorale utilizzati dal segretario al Tesoro statunitense rivelano la sua profonda disperazione di fronte alla forza dell'Iran", ha aggiunto Ghalibaf, citato dall'agenzia iraniana Irna.

Cicr, gli Houthi in Yemen rilasciano 600 combattenti filo-iraniani

Il Comitato internazionale della Croce Rossa (Cicr) ha annunciato la liberazione, da parte degli Houthi yemeniti filo-iraniani, di 600 membri delle forze governative che erano detenuti dalla ripresa delle ostilità a luglio. "Oggi, 600 persone detenute in relazione al conflitto in corso nello Yemen sono state rilasciate unilateralmente dalle autorità di Sana'a", ha dichiarato in un comunicato il Cicr, che ha assistito alle operazioni di rilascio. La commissione del movimento filo-iraniano che si occupa della questione dei prigionieri lo ha confermato.

Due petroliere sono esplose nello Stretto di Hormuz dopo aver urtato le mine

La Marina delle Guardie Rivoluzionarie in Iran ha reso noto che due petroliere - tra cui una superpetroliera - che stavano percorrendo una "rotta non autorizzata" nello Stretto di Hormuz hanno urtato delle mine, subendo violente esplosioni e prendendo fuoco. La superpetroliera, che trasportava oltre due milioni di barili di greggio, è affondata, ha aggiunto la fonte, citata dall'agenzia Tasnim.

Pasdaran rivendicano attacco a radar Usa in Bahrein con sei droni

I Pasdaran sostengono di aver colpito con sei droni il radar di un sistema di difesa aerea statunitense all'interno della base aerea di Riffa, in Bahrain. Lo riferisce l'agenzia iraniana Fars, vicina ai Guardiani della rivoluzione, citata da Al Jazeera. La rivendicazione è arrivata mentre nel Paese risuonavano le sirene e il ministero dell'Interno diffondeva allerte per una potenziale minaccia. Le autorità di Manama hanno invitato la popolazione a mantenere la calma e a raggiungere il rifugio più vicino. I Pasdaran hanno inoltre ribadito che lo Stretto di Hormuz resta chiuso, nonostante quello che Teheran ha definito il fallimento degli Stati Uniti nel tentativo di scortare le navi attraverso la via d'acqua. Qualsiasi nuova aggressione statunitense, hanno avvertito, riceverà una risposta "ancora più dura e devastante".

articles.title: Daily life in Sudan paralysed by deepening fuel crisis and rising costs

articles.preview: Sudan A deepening fuel crisis is paralysing daily life across Sudan, where long lines of vehicles at the few operating petrol stations have become a daily routine. Sudan

A deepening fuel crisis is paralysing daily life across Sudan, where long lines of vehicles at the few operating petrol stations have become a daily routine.

Amid the ongoing civil war, domestic refining has been crippled by drone attacks targeting infrastructure and energy and fuel sources.

At the time, conflict in the Middle East since late February has led to significant fluctuations in international energy market prices.

In his car at a petrol garage, Osman Faisal, a Khartoum resident, said he had started queuing for petrol at seven in the morning and had been waiting for over two hours.

"I don't know how much longer I'll have to wait. I haven't been able to fill up for a week,” he said.

“And the price of gasoline has further gone up recently. Now it costs about $58 per gallon. It has increased by over $8 in just several days."

The external shock of global oil prices has been exacerbated by the depreciation of the Sudanese pound against the US dollar, making every imported shipment more expensive.

Another Khartoum resident queuing for petrol, Adnan Osman, said he hoped the exchange rate would stabilise as soon as possible.

"Every morning when we wake up, we are forced to make a choice - go to work or queue for petrol," he said.

In addition to disrupting people's travel, the fuel shortage has driven up transportation and delivery costs, pushing the price of food and daily necessities higher.

"The prices of food, including vegetables and bread, are also on the rise. The life of everyone in this country is being severely affected," said resident Alrazy Mohamed.

It is also impacting the economy and is contributing to a worsening of the country’s humanitarian crisis.

Relentless clashes since fighting erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have forced major oil fields to shut down.

The Khartoum refinery, which once met about 70 per cent of national fuel needs, has closed and several oil fields are also offline, forcing Sudan to rely almost entirely on imports.

Caught between rising global prices and a plummeting local currency, petrol station operators are forced to constantly recalculate their rates and frequently shut down pumps.

articles.body:
Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.

An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.

Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.

“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.

The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.

Tit-for-tat attacks

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.

Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.

Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.

US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.

However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

articles.summary: 'Zionist regime's false flag': Iran warns France over supermarket cyberattack Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 11/15/2026 - 08:59 Paris has accused an IRGC-linked cyber unit of targeting refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets A woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarche supermarket in Nevez, western France, after a cyberattack disrupted refrigeration systems on 12 October 2026 (Fred Tanneau/AFP) Off Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned France against falling into an Israeli “false flag” trap after Paris accused an Iranian cyber unit of attacking refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets. IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi dismissed the French allegations as “ridiculous”, accusing Israel of seeking to turn European countries against Tehran and secure their support. “Paris should beware of the Zionist regime's false flag trap,” Mohebbi wrote on X on Saturday. He also said that, unlike the United States and Israel, the IRGC did not target civilians. France accused Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit within the IRGC’s Electronic Warfare and Cyber Defence Organisation, of carrying out the cyber attacks. The attacks targeted refrigeration control systems at over 700 retail outlets on the night of 11-12 October, causing fires, serious damage and losses of food worth tens of millions of euros, the French foreign ministry said. Paris said it would summon Iran's ambassador and propose new sanctions against individuals and entities within the European Union. Iran refuses to surrender enriched uranium, threatens to strike US bases in Europe if attacked ed and that Tehran would take steps to safeguard its national interests and security against illegal actions by foreign countries. The dispute comes amid a continuing confrontation between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz. On Sunday, Tehran claimed to have attacked a US radar site in Bahrain. The IRGC said it attacked a US air defence radar station with six drones at Riffa Air Base, Iranian state media said. Bahrain's interior ministry issued several warnings about the potential threat and advised locals to take cover. The claim follows a similar announcement by the IRGC on Friday that it had destroyed a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain. US Central Command (Centcom) rejected Friday’s account, saying American forces had intercepted two Iranian attack drones heading towards Bahrain. It reported no injuries or damage. Tanker fires The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has also deteriorated, with Iran reporting that oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to pass through the waterway. The IRGC Navy said early on Sunday that two tankers had exploded and caught fire after striking mines south of the strait. It accused the vessels of attempting to pass through an unauthorised route with their navigation and automatic identification systems switched off. The announcement followed reports on Saturday of two similar incidents involving tankers in the southern part of the waterway. Reuters reported that Iranian state media had described three tankers catching fire after striking mines on Saturday, including one in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC Navy has warned shipping companies against transiting the strait without coordinating with its maritime traffic control centre. articles.body:
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta, in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

articles.body:
The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.

The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.

Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.

“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.

A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.

Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.

“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.

During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.

The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.

This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

The former general is separately being investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.

More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.

A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.

“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

articles.title: Sudan: Misery worsens amid plummeting aid for displaced people
articles.summary: Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.
articles.preview: November 14, 2026 Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan.
articles.body:
November 14, 2026

Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan. Without urgent provision of flexible funding, even more families will have to cope without adequate protection from extreme weather conditions, insecurity, violence and exploitation in the coming months.

According to a recently published joint statement, $2.9 billion (€2.62bn) is needed for the United Nation's Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. This funding is intended to provide life-saving aid to 20.4 million people in Sudan. So far, however, only 47% of the required funds have been raised.

A total of 33.7 million people in the war- and famine-stricken country are dependent on humanitarian aid. Some 15.4 million alone require emergency shelter and basic household items. However, due to a lack of funding, aid organizations have been able to assist only 10%.

More than three and a half years after the war began between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is still the site of the world's largest humanitarian and displacement crisis. About 8.6 million people fled within the country to escape the escalating violence and more than 4.6 million fled to neighboring countries. Another 5.2 million have returned to their regions of origin despite the ongoing war. However, their towns and infrastructure have been destroyed. Fighting, drone strikes and logistical problems further complicate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

Between 40,000 and 250,000 people have been killed. Accurate or updated figures are not available as fighting continues, satellite-based internet communication is curbed, and many aid organizations and observers have left the country.

Donors cut back on funding

"It's hard to imagine how people are supposed to survive," Marina Peter, chairwoman of the Sudan and South Sudan Forum in Germany, told DW. In large parts of the country, people have been cut off from humanitarian aid since the war began. Some have survived by eating roots. According to the Sudan expert, the fact that people are still returning to war zones from neighboring countries is also linked to shortages: Food rations have been drastically cut in refugee camps.

Ivo Körner, Sudan specialist at Caritas International, criticizes the international community for the sharp decline in aid. "Globally, we're seeing a dramatic drop in funding for humanitarian aid," Körner told DW. It's not just the United States that has slashed its contributions; Germany and the European Union are also providing significantly less funding than they did four or five years ago, he said.

In Sudan, Caritas International supports refugees and the communities hosting them with cash assistance, drinking water supplies, basic medical care and seeds. However, Sudan's Caritas' projects in 2026 have been financed exclusively through donations. While Körner hopes for additional funding from the German Foreign Office for Sudan projects, he predicts that funding opportunities will be significantly more limited than in previous years.

According to Sudan expert Marina Peters, the consequences of the crisis are becoming increasingly difficult to assess. "In many parts of the country, people have already been completely cut off from humanitarian aid since the start of the war," she told DW. Peter also notes that child mortality in Sudan is above average. However, it is nearly impossible to determine the actual extent of the crisis more precisely because the warring parties continue to obstruct humanitarian access.

Who should take action?

On October 23, the United Kingdom and 31 other international partners, including Germany, issued a joint statement on the looming famine in Sudan. According to the statement, 19.5 million people — about 41% of the population — are suffering from acute food insecurity. The countries are calling on the warring parties to allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure. At the same time, they are demanding an increase in international aid funding.

While Marina Peter welcomes the appeal in principle, she sees a contradiction. "The question is: Who is this appeal actually directed at?" Most of the signatories have themselves systematically cut funding for humanitarian aid and development cooperation. The appeal to the international donor community is thus ultimately directed at the states themselves.

Meanwhile, the Sudanese government based in the country's capital Khartoum — led by General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan's SAF — rejects all warnings of a famine.

In a statement dated October 26, it claims that the food situation in the country is reportedly reassuring and that government reserves and ongoing agricultural production are sufficient to meet demand. According to Khartoum, the warnings from Western countries amount to a politicization of the humanitarian situation.

Peter criticized this statement as "truly cynical and almost perfidious. The government's claim that humanitarian organizations have unrestricted access also does not reflect reality, she said. In many places, aid continues to be obstructed.

Drone attacks exacerbate dangers

In addition to hunger and displacement, the threat to civilians posed by the use of drones is also growing. The Peace for Sudan Platform issued an appeal on November 5 calling for an end to attacks on civilians, markets, hospitals, and water and electricity supplies. In the first three weeks of October alone, at least 306 people were killed in attacks. According to the UN Human Rights Office, drones claimed the lives of at least 1,120 civilians in the first half of 2026.

"Drone strikes are a major problem," Caritas' Körner confirmed. They cause widespread anxiety among the population and often strike civilians. Added to this is the danger to humanitarian workers. This makes local partner organizations all the more important, he said. They enjoy the trust of the local population, are deeply rooted in the regions and in some cases are able to reach areas that international aid workers can hardly access.

This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Che cosa sta facendo l’Italia per difendersi dagli attacchi informatici
articles.summary: I numeri sono in aumento e negli ultimi anni sono state introdotte nuove regole e stanziate risorse per prevenire e contrastare le minacce. Ma capire quanto queste misure abbiano funzionato non è semplice
articles.preview: L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.
articles.body:
L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.

Questi episodi si inseriscono in un quadro che ha riportato l’attenzione sulle minacce informatiche e la capacità dell’Italia di contrastarle efficacemente. Il 7 novembre il ministero degli Esteri aveva reso nota la diffusione sul dark web di dati personali del ministro Antonio Tajani. Il Ministro ha collegato le minacce alla posizione italiana sulla guerra in Ucraina e ha chiesto di affrontare il tema delle minacce ibride al G7 degli Esteri, che si è svolto a Parigi il 9 e 10 novembre. Un altro episodio era stato registrato a inizio novembre, quando alcuni supermercati italiani erano stati colpiti da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione, sui cui il governo aveva fatto il punto in una riunione il 3 novembre.

Il 9 novembre il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto, in un’intervista al Corriere della Sera, ha definito la guerra ibrida una «sfida epocale», che deve essere affrontata tramite una strategia comune tra le istituzioni. Una posizione in linea con quanto detto qualche giorno dalla presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni, che aveva richiamato l’attenzione sui possibili effetti degli attacchi informatici, sottolineando i rischi per le infrastrutture civili.

Negli ultimi anni, l’Italia ha introdotto nuove regole, istituito strutture dedicate alla cybersicurezza e stanziato risorse per proteggere le proprie infrastrutture digitali. Ma quali interventi sono stati realizzati e che cosa dicono i dati disponibili sulla loro efficacia?

articles.title: Che cosa ha deciso la Corte costituzionale su Giusi Bartolozzi
articles.summary: È stato accolto solo in parte il conflitto di attribuzione sollevato dalla Camera, e ora l’ex capa di gabinetto di Nordio potrà essere processata per false dichiarazioni
articles.preview: Che cosa succede adesso La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali.
articles.body:
Che cosa succede adesso

La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. In quel caso, la Corte costituzionale dovrebbe verificare se la valutazione dei magistrati abbia leso le prerogative della Camera, non accertare la responsabilità penale di Bartolozzi.

Quanto alle presunte false informazioni, il procedimento prosegue secondo le regole ordinarie, senza necessità di autorizzazione parlamentare. La Procura ha già emesso un decreto di citazione diretta a giudizio nei confronti di Bartolozzi, che quindi potrà andare a processo.

Resta da chiarire se Bartolozzi avrebbe dovuto essere ascoltata come indagata, anziché come persona informata sui fatti. In quest’ultimo caso era tenuta a dire la verità, ed è proprio dalle dichiarazioni rese in questa veste che è nata l’accusa di false informazioni. Se fosse stata ascoltata come indagata, avrebbe invece avuto il diritto di non rispondere. La Corte costituzionale ha lasciato aperta la questione delle eventuali conseguenze sui suoi diritti di difesa. La procura prospetta, dal canto suo, un’altra eventualità: se nel corso del giudizio per false informazioni dovessero emergere indizi di concorso nei reati attribuiti a Nordio, il giudice dovrebbe assolvere Bartolozzi e restituire gli atti al pubblico ministero, per avviare la procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. Anche su questo profilo la Corte non si è pronunciata.

articles.body:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

I spoke to Leo Wang, the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai, this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

“If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing.

“If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”

Deals!

May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.)

Newmo, a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI.

ParkBee, a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations.

Port, an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord.

Notable reads and other tidbits

Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District.

The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end, according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker.

Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

United Airlines will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf.

articles.title: Le aziende costruttrici di data center non stanno andando bene
articles.summary: Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato il settore a un grosso calo in borsa
articles.preview: Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato il settore a un grosso calo in borsa L’autorevole quotidiano finanziario Financial Times ha scritto che il settore delle aziende legate alla costruzione di data center ha perso 4.200 miliardi di dollari di valore in borsa negli ultimi sei mesi. È quasi la metà del valore che aveva raggiunto nei 12 mesi precedenti: 9.400 miliardi. Il Financial Times scrive che è un calo dovuto al «vacillare della fiducia degli investitori nel boom dell’intelligenza artificiale».
articles.body:
Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato il settore a un grosso calo in borsa

L’autorevole quotidiano finanziario Financial Times ha scritto che il settore delle aziende legate alla costruzione di data center ha perso 4.200 miliardi di dollari di valore in borsa negli ultimi sei mesi. È quasi la metà del valore che aveva raggiunto nei 12 mesi precedenti: 9.400 miliardi. Il Financial Times scrive che è un calo dovuto al «vacillare della fiducia degli investitori nel boom dell’intelligenza artificiale».

Le aziende di cui parla il Financial Times non sono quelle tecnologiche che si occupano di hardware e software per l’intelligenza artificiale, ma quelle che forniscono energia e materiali per la costruzione dei centri. Cita per esempio Caterpillar, il principale fornitore di generatori a gas per i data center, la produttrice di energia nucleare Oklo, l’azienda che produce sistemi di raffreddamento Comfort Systems e quella di tecnologie ottiche Corning. Tutte, scrive il Financial Times, da giugno hanno perso più del 40 per cento del loro valore in borsa.

All’origine di tutto c’è l’enorme crescita del settore dell’intelligenza artificiale – e quindi dei data center – che fino a qualche mese fa aveva spinto gli investitori a comprare azioni di queste aziende in previsione di un continuo aumento dei cantieri. Negli ultimi mesi le cose però sono un po’ cambiate e molti hanno venduto quelle azioni portando a un crollo del valore di mercato delle aziende.

I data center sono grossi stabilimenti industriali pieni di computer, server, cavi e infrastrutture digitali, di cui le aziende tecnologiche hanno bisogno per far funzionare i loro servizi. La loro costruzione è diventata urgente e fondamentale con lo sviluppo di modelli di intelligenza artificiale sempre più avanzati, che per funzionare richiedono data center sempre più performanti.

Ultimamente però i data center hanno cominciato ad avere una pessima reputazione. Negli Stati Uniti l’ostilità per la loro costruzione è una delle poche cose che ha messo d’accordo Democratici e Repubblicani alle ultime elezioni di metà mandato. Ma proteste contro le nuove costruzioni sono state organizzate anche in altri paesi negli ultimi mesi. Oltre a richiedere cantieri enormi, i data center sono infatti spesso rumorosi e richiedono grandi quantità di energia, che viene così sottratta alle comunità vicine.

– Leggi anche: Le proteste contro i data center sono arrivate anche in Italia

Oltre a questo c’è la grande prudenza legata al timore che il settore delle AI si riveli una bolla, dal momento che finora si è basato su enormi investimenti che però non hanno ancora permesso alle aziende di guadagnare altrettanto. È a questo che ci si riferisce quando si parla di «sfiducia nel settore delle AI»: più si va avanti e più l’incertezza cresce. Recentemente per esempio è uscita la notizia che in Cina le aziende che sviluppano modelli di AI hanno subito pesanti perdite.

Tra gli esperti sentiti dal Financial Times c’è chi sostiene che il calo del valore di queste aziende in borsa non significhi che il settore della costruzione di data center non sia in crescita e che questo sia dimostrato dalla quantità di ordini che le aziende continuano a ricevere; altri fanno notare invece come gli ordini non siano un indicatore rappresentativo, perché è il risultato di valutazioni ormai vecchie e che potrebbero essere state superate.

Bisogna anche vedere se negli Stati Uniti cambierà qualcosa nella normativa, dal momento che la lotta ai data center è stato uno dei temi più centrali delle campagne di politici locali e nazionali che sono stati eletti alle ultime elezioni.
