articles.body:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Things moved fast for the now-former CEO of Nvidia.

How it started

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously told The Verge. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.”

The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing.

This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even putting him on speakerphone on-stage at the All-In Summit.

Then last week, things escalated quickly.

On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature.

On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after.

Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.)

Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.”

On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

How it’s going

CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.”

But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It closed at $162.85 on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure.

Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair.

By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair, this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged.

What happens next

First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire Tim Cook, but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.)

It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward.

The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is likely to drag on for some time. With the possibility that Jensen Huang will have to testify before Congress, the company may choose to be proactive about disclosing any additional information publicly.

The incoming Democratic majority is expected to come down harder on Silicon Valley than the current Republican Congress. While it’s unclear just how far the new House and Senate will go in trying to rein in the tech industry and its billionaire leaders, it’s possible it will try to make an example of Nvidia as an early act of strength. If Nvidia is found to have been turning a blind eye to companies like Megaspeed, which are suspected of funneling advanced chips to China, it could face civil or criminal penalties. And it seems increasingly likely that stricter trade restrictions will be implemented on Nvidia’s chips, which could increase tensions with China in an already costly trade war.

There is a possibility that Jensen Huang could face criminal charges. In May, he claimed that Nvidia had “zero percent” market share in China due to stringent export restrictions. But shortly after, Culper Research published a report claiming that in reality over 20 percent of the company’s 2026 compute revenue was from China, though that number has not been independently verified. The report cited “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries” as the primary source of those revenues. Among the largest of those intermediaries, according to Culper Research, was Megaspeed, which Nvidia repeatedly vouched for to the US government.

If proof is established that the CEO was knowingly helping Megaspeed or any other companies to illegally divert restricted chips to China, he could face criminal charges. And, as The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto put it, “under a functioning legal system, [he] could actually go to jail.”

There is the chance that members of the current administration are also tied up in this scandal, as it’s unclear how much the White House knew and when.

Considering Nvidia’s sizable investments, borrowing to build data centers, and the importance of its hardware, there are tons of open questions about how this impacts not just the AI industry, but the American economy as a whole. Nvidia is essentially propping up a large part of the tech industry and, if money stops flowing out of its coffers, it could drag a lot of other companies down with it.

There are also open questions about how this impacts the American public’s perception of the AI industry. The new Democratic majority was elected in part by campaigning against AI companies and the explosion of data center buildout across the country. That one of its more prominent CEOs is now embroiled in a spying scandal and multiple extramarital affairs probably isn’t going to endear the industry to the public.

By the way

- Megaspeed was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, but when Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited its office in October of 2025, it found “no signs of activity.”

- Megaspeed is just one of multiple companies that Nvidia has been approved to sell chips with suspicious offices. The New York Times described New Matrix’s headquarters as “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.”

- Jensen Huang’s connections to Super Micro are also under scrutiny. Earlier this year, one of its founders, an employee, and a contractor for the company were indicted by the Justice Department for conspiring to violate American export controls and divert Nvidia chips to China.

Read this

- While a lot has changed, it’s still worth reading the Times’ first big report from October 29th that lays the groundwork for the eventual deluge of international intrigue and infidelity that ultimately led to Jensen Huang’s downfall.

- The New York Times paints a fascinating portrait of Alice Huang who now finds herself at the center of an international espionage scandal.

- The Decoder interview with Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, digs into what China hoped to get out of Jensen Huang.

Le accuse sono di accesso abusivo a sistema informatico, detenzione e diffusione abusiva di codici di accesso, diffusione di strumenti per danneggiare sistemi informatici, intercettazione illecita di comunicazioni telematiche, sostituzione di persona, frode informatica e ricettazione. Oltre ad usare i sistemi, secondo l'accusa, i due insegnavano agli altri a farlo distribuendo consigli e video tutorial. Tra i materiali recuperati attraverso i loro dispositivi, c'erano anche manuali su come clonare carte di credito e come accreditarsi su un portale del ministero della giustizia, utilizzando il nome di un carabiniere realmente esistente. articles.title: Cosa sappiamo delle accuse di contrabbando ad Alice Huang
articles.summary: Di lei si è parlato soprattutto come sospetta spia cinese, ma i suoi traffici di chip potrebbero essere un problema altrettanto grave per l'ex CEO di Nvidia Jensen Huang
articles.preview: Abbiamo parlato di spionaggio, ora parliamo di contrabbando L'amante cinese dell'ex CEO di Nvidia era indagata da tempo per le quantità di chip che importava in Asia Il dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti aveva cominciato a indagare sull’imprenditrice cinese Alice Huang nel 2024, ben prima che venisse fuori la sua relazione con l’ex CEO di Nvidia Jensen Huang, dimessosi giovedì, e ancora prima che si cominciasse a parlare di lei come di una possibile spia del governo cinese.
articles.body:
Abbiamo parlato di spionaggio, ora parliamo di contrabbando

L'amante cinese dell'ex CEO di Nvidia era indagata da tempo per le quantità di chip che importava in Asia

Il dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti aveva cominciato a indagare sull’imprenditrice cinese Alice Huang nel 2024, ben prima che venisse fuori la sua relazione con l’ex CEO di Nvidia Jensen Huang, dimessosi giovedì, e ancora prima che si cominciasse a parlare di lei come di una possibile spia del governo cinese.

Il motivo è che Megaspeed, un’azienda di data center di Singapore fondata nel 2023 e di cui Alice Huang è stata dirigente, è sospettata di aver gestito il contrabbando di microchip di Nvidia, tra i più potenti al mondo per l’intelligenza artificiale, di cui gli Stati Uniti vietano l’esportazione in Cina dal 2022.

Huang non sarebbe la prima: che microchip avanzati prodotti negli Stati Uniti arrivino in Cina di contrabbando aggirando i controlli sulle esportazioni è noto. Negli ultimi anni il dipartimento di Giustizia ha incriminato diverse persone per averli fatti passare illegalmente attraverso paesi del sudest asiatico. Quello che rende questo caso eccezionale è l’eventuale ruolo che avrebbe avuto Jensen Huang, cittadino statunitense e capo di una delle più importanti aziende tecnologiche del paese.

Il Wall Street Journal ha scritto sabato che «Jensen Huang ha costruito un business multimilionario per nutrire il vorace appetito di chip americani dei clienti cinesi». E che lo scandalo che ha portato alle sue dimissioni minaccia ora di far implodere «l’ecosistema lucrativo che [Nvidia] ha costruito in Asia».

Breve riassunto della questione: Nvidia ha il monopolio di fatto nella progettazione di GPU, chip avanzatissimi che negli ultimi anni si sono rivelati fondamentali per lo sviluppo dei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale. Negli Stati Uniti il blocco alle esportazioni di chip verso la Cina era stato imposto prima dall’amministrazione di Joe Biden e poi da quella di Donald Trump, con lo scopo di contrastare il progresso tecnologico cinese.

Per Nvidia questo aveva portato molte perdite, e infatti Jensen Huang aveva provato a lungo a convincere Trump a modificare le norme sull’esportazione di chip. I due hanno un ottimo rapporto e Huang aveva ottenuto alcuni allentamenti, ma mai l’eliminazione completa del divieto. Per aggirarlo, le aziende cinesi hanno trovato due soluzioni: appoggiarsi legalmente a data center fuori dalla Cina, spesso nel sudest asiatico, oppure importare illegalmente i microchip con vari trucchi.

Alice Huang è diventata dirigente di Megaspeed nel 2023: da filiale di una società cinese di videogiochi online, Huang redirezionò gli investimenti dell’azienda sui data center. Ufficialmente non faceva nulla di illegale: Megaspeed importava i chip statunitensi e affittava la potenza di calcolo ad aziende cinesi senza muovere i chip in Cina. Tra i suoi clienti c’era Alibaba, la prima azienda di e-commerce cinese.

Secondo quanto ipotizzato dalle indagini e da alcune inchieste giornalistiche però Megaspeed non si sarebbe limitata ad affittare la potenza di calcolo, ma sarebbe diventata uno snodo del contrabbando. Per dirigere questo traffico Alice Huang avrebbe sfruttato anche la sua vicinanza a Jensen Huang. Su di lei ci sono indagini in corso da tempo, mentre sul ruolo che Jensen Huang e Nvidia potrebbero aver avuto in tutto questo si sa ancora poco.

Un indizio a sostegno delle accuse a Megaspeed è la quantità di chip che l’azienda aveva comprato negli ultimi anni, per il valore di diversi miliardi di dollari. Una quantità giudicata eccessiva per gli scopi e l’estensione delle sue attività.

Stando a un’esclusiva del New York Times, già nel 2024 questa quantità fece nascere dei sospetti e il dipartimento del Commercio statunitense inviò dei funzionari in un data center di Megaspeed in Malaysia, per verificare che i microchip venduti fossero davvero lì. Li trovò, ma erano ancora negli imballaggi, cosa che fece nascere il sospetto che i chip transitassero dal data center ma poi venissero inviati in Cina.

Venerdì Bloomberg ha scritto che, secondo documenti di cui è venuto in possesso, un’azienda cinese fondata da Alice Huang nel 2015 si sarebbe procurata chip di Nvidia arrivati in Cina di contrabbando, poi installati in un data center di Shanghai legato a Megaspeed. Bloomberg dice che ci sono evidenze per dire che i microchip siano stati importati per «una larga rete di aziende con al centro Alice Huang».

Venerdì il segretario al Tesoro Scott Bessent ha accusato pubblicamente il dipartimento del Commercio e il suo segretario, Howard Lutnick, di non aver agito tempestivamente per inserire Megaspeed nell’elenco delle aziende che non possono acquistare prodotti tecnologici dalle società statunitensi senza una precedente approvazione da parte del governo.

Sempre secondo un’inchiesta del New York Times, Nvidia avrebbe avuto un ruolo nel mancato intervento del dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti, che pure aveva incominciato a indagare sulle attività di contrabbando di Megaspeed e Alice Huang nel 2024.

Secondo il New York Times, ad agosto dell’anno scorso Tim Teter, il consulente legale generale di Nvidia, contattò direttamente alcuni agenti del dipartimento del Commercio coinvolti nell’indagine su Megaspeed, chiedendo loro di incontrarli per parlare del caso: la cosa insolita è che nella mail diceva di aveva ricevuto il permesso di contattarli dal loro capo, Jeff Kessler, uno dei principali dirigenti del dipartimento, nominato da Trump.

Nonostante la pressione legata al nome di Kessler, gli agenti del dipartimento del Commercio negarono a Teter l’incontro, ma non ebbero tempo di pensare ulteriormente a come gestire la cosa perché l’indagine gli fu tolta, e fu spostata al dipartimento di Giustizia dove è ancora in corso. Dell’indagine del dipartimento di Giustizia non si sa al momento niente.

Il New York Times ha scritto che «non è chiaro cosa abbia spinto il signor Teter a rivolgersi al dipartimento, ma le recenti rivelazioni sulla relazione ammessa da Jansen Huang con una dirigente di Megaspeed non hanno fatto altro che aumentare l’attenzione sul ruolo di Nvidia nell’influenzare le politiche relative alla vendita di chip alla Cina».

Non è chiaro se Jensen Huang fosse al corrente della presunta attività di contrabbando di Megaspeed, e se sia intervenuto per facilitarla e ostacolare le indagini del dipartimento del Commercio, ma se dovesse venire fuori che è successo sarebbe uno scandalo enorme, non solo per Nvidia ma soprattutto per il governo statunitense.

articles.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
articles.summary: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.preview: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.body:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)

Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”

It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

articles.body:
November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. CSET’s Helen Toner says ‘we’re screwed’ if our AI safety plan rests on any one person being trusted to get this right. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. My view of the idea of slowing down has changed a lot over the years as the backlog of stuff that we could try or stuff that we would want to do more research on has grown so enormous. Back when GPT-4 came out, there was the six-month pause letter, which became known as the “Elon Musk Letter” because he was one of the signatories. At the time, I thought, “That’s really not going to help. What are you going to do for six months and why are things going to be better six months from now? It doesn’t seem useful.” Whereas today, when I talk to people who are building this technology, they say, “Man, the amount that we could do in six months if we weren’t constantly just trying to prep for a new model release or a new training run to be kicked off.” There’s so much they could do. So I don’t want to say the correct policy is to pause for six months. I think there are a lot of reasons that would go badly. But I think about the overall concept of, “Can we give ourselves more attention and time?” Maybe the best way to do that is just to set a higher bar for “here’s how confident we need to be in the safety of these systems before we proceed with something.” Whether it’s releasing a new model or, more importantly, even training a new model, we have to have this level of confidence in our risk assessment and our risk management. And then if they don’t need to slow down to reach that bar, great, carry on full speed ahead. If they do need to take more time, then it’s all about reaching that bar, if that makes sense. Walk me through that little balance you just described. If we were to pause for some number of months, what are the things on the list that you could just do to make everything safer and why would it go badly such that we shouldn’t just stop? I think the question is how do you implement, and how do you enforce, a pause and what exactly are you pausing? Let’s say you’re the AI czar of America. So let’s say you can tell them all to stop: “Dario, shut it down.” Stop what though? What specifically are they stopping? Stop training the next model, stop racing ahead with your commercial imperatives. Put all of your efforts on this list of things you can do today to make everything safer before you start again, for however long. You’re saying that there’s a list, that people would tell you that there is a list, but it might not be worth it because something else would happen that is bad. Yeah. One thing that could happen is you’re creating a huge incentive for the companies to work around the letter of whatever specific thing you tell them to pause. They’re going to find whatever cracks in the dam that they can to push through that. A different thing that could happen is you could have too big a blast radius, so you say “pause these things” and you think it’s pretty narrow, but actually it prevents a bunch of nonprofit products or startups or other actors from doing work that actually would be totally fine and would be good for pluralism and dynamism in the space. A different thing that would happen is China would probably keep going, and we can talk about the “But China” argument, which I think has strengths and weaknesses. But I take your point. Your point is, what would we actually do? I am not an AI researcher, so I don’t claim to have the full list. There are two halves people talk about, which are alignment and control. In this breakdown, alignment basically means making it so the models are trying to do what we want them to do, and control is, if the models are trying to do something we didn’t want them to do, can we catch them? Can we stop them? In both of these, as I understand it, there’s just a huge backlog of things, like all kinds of interpretability work that you could do on different sorts of models. So when you see a certain behavior that is concerning, how much time can you spend using interpretability techniques, which are these mathematical techniques to go in and look at which parts of the neural network are activated and what do they correlate with and what might that mean? It’s just time-consuming and it takes compute and it takes some combination of automating things with AI and then humans going in and looking at it. There are lots of tests you could do to see what kinds of behaviors this new model displays in different kinds of situations and how we think about it. Is it showing us how it would behave in the wild in a real deployment, or is it showing us what gets called “evaluation awareness,” which is when the model recognizes that it’s in a test and then behaves differently because it’s in a test. The famous one, the one that I love, is of this Google model, which in part of its reasoning, its chain of thought, said,, “I mustn’t do that, otherwise I’ll become a famous example of a misaligned AI in a paper.” So you could go in and investigate that much more. You could try many more different types of settings. You could use interpretability in combination with these different settings. You could try out different ways of fine-tuning the models and these different sorts of alignment techniques. You could experiment with lots of different versions. Anthropic has its constitution, and there are different ways of training the AI to work towards the constitution. OpenAI has its model spec. They’re both the “just try things” version, just try many different versions of how to train to do those different things. Also, the more underlying science version of, “How can you go in there and try to understand the fundamental dynamics of what’s happening?” That’s just on the alignment side. So then on the control side, it’s the same thing. There are so many different types of setups you could try. There are experiments that you could run. There are simulations you could run. You could train different types of AI to specialize in different types of roles and different types of control setups. This is just off the top of my head, not as a researcher, but my understanding is the people in these spaces say, “We could do so, so, so much.” They could do that if you just had a magic wand and waved it and said, “Everyone freeze on the new capability side and just let these people do their thing.” Again, if you’re just having a higher bar for how confident we need to be that the risk is being managed reasonably, then that would also create space and incentives for more of that work to be done as it’s needed for new training and releases. One idea that I’ve heard you talk about in the past is that maybe we should just restrict training and say the models are good enough right now. They have not diffused into society and we should just use all the compute for inference and let everyone figure out what the AI is for. That’ll generate a bunch of money and hopefully use that money to improve safety. Do you think that’s a realistic policy proposal? I wouldn’t go for that black-and-white a version of “no more training, only inference,” but I do think that there’s… this isn’t my framing, but I like it. I think this idea of decelerating the vertical growth of AI, meaning the pure capabilities growth, making more and more and more advanced AI models, but trying to accelerate the horizontal growth, meaning integrating AI into different use cases, fine-tuning models that could solve specific problems, integrating it into parts of the economy that might take longer, and solving scientific problems. Sometimes people talk about wanting to slow down AI and they mean just the very specific thing of slowing down the growth of the most advanced models, but people sometimes take them to mean slowing down everything to do with AI. So less deployment, less experimentation, less integration, which I think would be a much worse idea. You asked if it is feasible, I think. Well, is that just a good path? If we could put a bill in front of our new Congress and the bill said, “Stop spending all the money on training and put all your resources on safety.” Part of that is, “Sure, let it rip on inference. More and more industries will figure out what AI is good for and not good for. Some bad things will happen, but we will focus your profits on fixing the things for now.” There’s a policy idea embedded in there that is workable. The implementation might be very challenging, but it’s a workable policy idea. Actually, I’ll give you an example that I’ve been thinking about as we’ve been talking. We just had Bill Gates on the show, and I tried to do the same exercise with him. What is the nature of the technology? What is the nature of the companies? Do you think it’s alive? Basically, his response, the sum total of that hour I spent with him, was, “Who cares? The problem is now.” I would ask him, “What is the nature of AI?” And he’s like, “I don’t give a shit. Everything’s going to get ruined. Do something.” That’s just been swirling in my head as we’ve been talking. So one workable policy solution is “don’t use the computer chips for that, use the computer chips for this. That’s going to create a bunch of problems and necessarily we will have to create safety thresholds and all the other stuff.” And then you can go make the next generation of models that are even more powerful and we’ll have some muscles. We’ll have some capability to deal with it. It just doesn’t seem like the industry is going to come to that conclusion on its own. It’s a pretty heavy hammer. I don’t feel like it’s what we need today, but I do think it’s the kind of thing that I could imagine working. Again, if the OpenAI and Anthropic people are right and we only have two years before the god machine, then I think we’re going to have a number more steps in the pipeline of people getting freaked out and people wanting to do something about it. I think if we are seeing models that are agents and systems that are getting more and more capable and wreaking more and more havoc, then that is certainly the shape of things that could make sense. My last question in this phase is what to make of these companies. We’ve been talking about the technology in a very abstract way. If I read Anthropic’s S-1, one very obvious conclusion is they should stop training new models. They should just start selling the very lucrative inference tokens they have today and the technology is not diffused into the market and probably some competitor should come along and be like, “I’ve distilled a version of Claude and I’m going to run around every local plumbing business in America and do whatever automation I can for lots and lots of money.” That is a market dynamic that may occur or may not. But Dario wants to build AGI. There’s not a market dynamic that’s going to stop him from that. Yeah, he really does. He really, really does. You obviously have insight into all these companies. What do we make of the companies? Are they single-minded in purpose? Are they all doomers? Are they going to stop themselves? I heard you had Kevin Roose on your podcast recently, and I think I would echo something that I heard him saying there, which I forget if he said it explicitly or if I just extrapolated it in my head, which is basically there’s this sort of AGI-pilled mindset. There’s this mindset that the systems that we have today are not fundamentally very far away from systems that could be incredibly, incredibly powerful. That’s the direction things are going in and that’s the direction we should maybe want them to go in so that you’re building AGI. Building AGI is feasible and we could do it soon and the systems we have are not far away. That was this crazy, heretical, “get you laughed out of the room” kind of view in 2016 or 2017, and even before that, right? DeepMind, when it was founded in 2010, was an AGI company and at the time it was like, “Wow, what a bunch of weirdos.” The same thing was true of OpenAI when it was founded at the end of 2015. They were an AGI company and that was a very weird thing to say and a very weird thing to be. What we’ve seen over the past 10 years is that bunch of weirdos who had this weird belief that the AI systems we can build are not just great B2B SaaS products. They’re not just fun chatbots. They’re going to fundamentally change the nature of the universe. That group of people keeps being right in the sense of building the best AI systems that the most people want to use and that make the most money. I think you have that set of true believers — which is very concentrated in OpenAI and Anthropic, but there are also some of them at Google, Meta, and SpaceX — and they haven’t been right about everything, to be clear, but their star has risen. So you now have people who are not AGI-pilled feeling like they have to pander to those who are so that they can attract the good researchers who will build their good B2B SaaS products. But if you’re just saying AGI-pilled things so that you can hire the researchers to build the B2B SaaS, then you’re not actually going to get there.

articles.summary: The tech giant said on Saturday that service has now been restored across Teams, Outlook, and its other products, ending the shutdown.

articles.body:
Microsoft

Multinational technology corporation, Microsoft, has apologised for a global service outage that left millions of users unable to use its apps for more than 24 hours.

It said on Saturday that service has been restored across Teams, Outlook, and its other products, ending the shutdown that crippled online communications for businesses, governments, and individual users.

Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.

The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars, and hosting virtual meetings.

Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.

The outage was one of the longest in software giant’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.

The incident highlighted concerns about the world’s reliance on the company’s workplace software.

articles.body:
Per l’accesso alle foto sugli smartphone senza il consenso delle persone tramite l’applicazione di Facebook

Il Garante della Privacy ha fatto una multa da 805 milioni di euro a Meta, la società che possiede Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp, perché attraverso l’applicazione di Facebook per Android la società avrebbe avuto accesso a fotografie, video e relativi metadati conservati sulle gallerie dei telefoni delle persone, senza il loro consenso.

Il Garante, che controlla che vengano rispettate le normative nazionali ed europee sul trattamento dei dati personali, ha detto che la violazione ha riguardato un numero elevato di persone: non ha specificato quante, ma ha detto che ci sono 20 milioni di profili Facebook in Italia che usano l’app di Android.

Al centro dell’indagine che ha portato alla multa c’è la funzione “Ottieni suggerimenti dalla galleria quando navighi su Facebook”, inserita nel 2023, quella che propone agli utenti foto e video da pubblicare prendendoli dalla galleria del telefono. Il problema, secondo il Garante, è che Meta non ha richiesto un consenso specifico per accedere alla galleria tramite questa funzione, ma lo ha fatto usando il consenso generale, quello che gli utenti accettano per tutta l’app.

Inoltre secondo il Garante l’impostazione che permetteva alla app di accedere a tutto l’archivio fotografico di un dispositivo risultava attiva di default. In questo modo spettava alle persone accorgersi dell’impostazione e disattivarla nel momento in cui non l’avessero voluta. Il Garante della Privacy ha imposto a Meta di modificare le impostazioni e chiedere tutti i consensi corretti entro 60 giorni.

Meta ha contestato la ricostruzione dell’autorità italiana e ha fatto sapere che intende presentare ricorso. Meno di un mese fa l’azienda ha ricevuto una multa che, se confermata in tutti in gradi di giudizio, sarebbe la più alta tra quelle che ha dovuto pagare finora: un giudice del New Mexico, negli Stati Uniti, ha multato Meta per 25 miliardi di dollari per aver violato la privacy dei suoi utenti, in un caso relativo allo scandalo Cambridge Analytica, l’azienda di consulenza britannica che si era impossessata dei dati di decine di milioni di utenti in tutto il mondo in modo poco chiaro e a loro insaputa.

articles.body:
Nell’industria oltre nove su dieci con contratto in vigore, a fine anno scadono calzature, grafici e autoferrotranvieri. Nei servizi accordi in scadenza in marzo per i 3 milioni del commercio

Il fattore tempo incombe sulla tensione contrattuale, soprattutto nei servizi. In pochi mesi, nel privato, i lavoratori con il contratto scaduto, passeranno infatti dagli attuali 1,1 milioni, certificati dagli ultimi dati Istat, a ben oltre 4 milioni, in marzo, quando scadranno gli accordi del terziario che riguardano circa 3 milioni di addetti, dopo che a fine anno scadranno anche altre categorie, dagli autoferrotranvieri, ai calzaturieri ai grafici. Prendendo proprio gli ultimi dati Istat, complessivamente i dipendenti in attesa di rinnovo sono 2,5 milioni (tenuto conto anche degli 1,4 milioni del pubblico) circa il 19,2%, ossia uno su cinque, in forte calo rispetto a un anno fa: in settembre del 2025 erano il 43,1%. Dopo tanti passi avanti, grazie anche al pubblico, senza rinnovi in tempi fisiologici, già la prossima primavera si rischia di tornare indietro, ai tempi in cui quasi un lavoratore su due del privato, era in attesa del rinnovo del contratto.

La questione salariale riaperta dalla nuova dinamica dei prezzi, con l’inflazione che rialza la testa, dà al fattore tempo e alla parte economica dei rinnovi contrattuali ancora più centralità per consentire ai lavoratori in attesa del rinnovo del contratto di lavoro di recuperare il potere di acquisto. Lo è a tal punto da aver avuto una parte importante nell’accordo quadro sulla rappresentanza delle 13 associazioni datoriali (da Confindustria, a Confcommercio, alle Coop agli artigiani) con Cgil, Cisl e Uil. Le parti hanno condiviso di introdurre un meccanismo di protezione dei salari dalle fiammate inflattive, mentre il contratto è in vigore, con verifiche annuali o biennali per fare sì che ci sia un adeguamento periodico dei salari all’inflazione. Come già avviene nei contratti più d’avanguardia, tra cui quello dell’industria metalmeccanica. E ha sollecitato un’accelerazione delle tempistiche, con l’avvio rapido dei negoziati: le piattaforme andranno presentate sei mesi prima della scadenza, con risposta entro 30 giorni, proprio per evitare vacanze contrattuali.

Entrando nelle dinamiche del settore privato, l’industria ha la situazione più stabile. Se prendiamo i 6,1 milioni di lavoratori a cui si applicano i contratti del sistema Confindustria, distinti per scadenza, a fine ottobre sono quasi 5,8 milioni, ossia il 94,1% del totale gli addetti che hanno un contratto collettivo in vigore: dalla metalmeccanica alla chimica farmaceutica, alla gommaplastica di rinnovo si comincerà a parlare a 2028 inoltrato. Per 365mila lavoratori il contratto scadrà a fine 2026: stiamo parlando, per esempio, dei grafici, degli autoferrotranvieri e dei calzaturieri. Sono invece circa 100mila, gli addetti che hanno contratti scaduti da non molto tempo, comunque da meno di 12 mesi e su cui ci sono trattative in corso, come la vigilanza privata e la concia. A questa platea vanno sottratti i 50mila lavoratori del settore pelli e ombrelli che hanno rinnovato nei giorni scorsi il contratto con un aumento complessivo di 204 euro mensili, a regime. I ritardi più lunghi, superiori a 12 mesi, riguardano complessivamente circa 200mila lavoratori, ossia il 3,3% del totale. Tra questi ci sono i lavoratori della sanità privata, in particolare delle case di cura su cui è in corso una trattativa piuttosto complessa, soprattutto sul capitolo degli inquadramenti. Nel 2027 arriveranno a scadenza alcuni importanti contratti come la moda, in marzo, la ceramica in giugno, e gli alimentaristi in novembre. A seguire, a fine anno, sarà la volta di logistica, settore elettrico ed energia e petroli, tra gli altri.

Nei servizi c’è una certa vivacità. Questa settimana, Federdistribuzione e Filcams, Fisascat e Uiltucs hanno fatto le prove generali dell’accordo sulla rappresentanza. Nelle scorse settimane, i sindacati hanno presentato con oltre sei mesi di anticipo rispetto alla scadenza del prossimo marzo, una piattaforma unitaria a tutte le associazioni datoriali, da Confcommercio, a Confesercenti, alle Coop, a Federdistribuzione, con una richiesta di aumento di 220 euro mensili a regime, sollecitando tutte le associazioni di categoria ad avviare velocemente il negoziato per rinnovare per tempo i contratti che riguardano quasi 3 milioni di lavoratori. La prima a rispondere e a incontrarli è stata Federdistribuzione. Le altre mancano ancora all’appello. Non ci sono notizie, invece, ormai da molti mesi, del rinnovo dei lavoratori delle farmacie, scaduto nel 2024, mentre procedono gli incontri tra Abi e i sindacati per il rinnovo del contratto dei bancari, ormai in una fase interlocutoria da molti mesi, a cui i sindacati e i lavoratori sono sempre più insofferenti.

Del resto la dinamica inflattiva è molto forte ed entra nella quotidianità del carrello della spesa, delle utenze, del pieno di carburante, degli spostamenti, del tempo libero e dei consumi. In ottobre, gli energetici regolamentati sono passati da +25,9% a +59,5%, quelli non regolamentati da +22,5% a +29,4%. Questo ha fatto sì che secondo l’Istat l’indice Nic abbia registrato una variazione pari a +0,9% su base mensile e ben +5,4% su base annua, in crescita rispetto a settembre quando era +4,2% rispetto al mese precedente. E gli aumenti retributivi? Non tengono il passo. L’indice delle retribuzioni contrattuali orarie, a settembre 2026, rimane invariato rispetto al mese precedente e aumenta del 2,5% rispetto a settembre 2025; l’aumento tendenziale è stato del 2,3% nel settore privato (3,3% nell’agricoltura, 2,6% nell’industria e 2,1% nei servizi privati) e del 3,2% per la pubblica amministrazione. Siamo quindi al secondo mese di fila in cui nel complesso le retribuzioni crescono meno dell’inflazione, una dinamica che nel privato va avanti da aprile. Sugli aumenti contrattuali è intervenuta anche la manovra di bilancio che ha confermato la flat tax al 5% .

articles.body:
La conclusione del Pnrr apre un’incognita sulla fine del 2026. Intanto nei primi mesi dell’anno le esportazioni crescono del 15%: nonostante questo l’industria sconta una certa debolezza legata all’incertezza del contesto e alle prospettive dell’ex-Ilva

In Puglia export aumentato del 15% e Pil regionale dell’1%, complici gli investimenti del Pnrr. I dati del rapporto congiunturale di Bankitalia si riferiscono al primo semestre dell’anno, rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025 e sono in linea con quelli dell’Italia e del Sud, rispettivamente pari allo 0,9 e all’1%. La seconda parte dell’anno - si legge nel rapporto - prefigura invece un peggioramento, per effetto della conclusione del Pnrr, dell’aumento dell’inflazione, delle tensioni internazionali e dell’incertezza sul futuro della ex-Ilva.

Se la domanda interna è cresciuta in misura contenuta con un incremento moderato dei consumi e un andamento debole degli investimenti, la domanda estera si è invece rafforzata con una performance a doppia cifra. L’industria ha mostrato una crescita modesta - nonostante il forte recupero delle esportazioni - a causa dell’incertezza legata, appunto, alle prospettive dell’ex-Ilva. L’espansione è stata più intensa nel settore delle costruzioni, in particolare nelle opere pubbliche, e così nel terziario con l’andamento favorevole delle attività turistico-ricettive caratterizzate da una particolare incidenza di lavoro part time e stagionale, oltre che da un complessivo non alto valore aggiunto sull’economia regionale.

Quanto al Pnrr, i pagamenti in Puglia, a giugno 2026, sono stati pari a 5,7 miliardi di euro, il 54% delle risorse previste, a fronte di circa 4,4 miliardi dello scorso aprile. Rispetto al dato nazionale, la progressione è inferiore alla media italiana in tutte le missioni ed è più accentuata nella missione 3 “Infrastrutture per una mobilità sostenibile”.

Nel primo semestre del 2026 l’occupazione è risalita dello 0,6%, dopo il lieve calo del 2025, mentre ad aumentare è stato in particolare quello autonomo(1,9%). Il tasso di occupazione è cresciuto dello 0,7%, al 51,7%, e il divario con l’Italia è rimasto sostanzialmente invariato a 11,3 punti.

«La ripresa - spiega Marcello Malamisura, direttore della sede di Bari di Bankitalia - si è associata però ad un ulteriore incremento della diffusione degli ammortizzatori sociali, che resta più elevata rispetto alla media nazionale anche per il perdurare di alcune importanti crisi aziendali, tra cui quella del polo siderurgico tarantino». Il potere d’acquisto è aumentato in misura contenuta: l’espansione si è concentrata nei primi 3 mesi diventando lievemente negativa nel secondo trimestre, a causa del rialzo dell’inflazione. Per quanto riguarda, invece, i finanziamenti alle famiglie, hanno continuato a crescere con intensità simile a quella della fine dello scorso anno: all’accelerazione del credito al consumo si è contrapposto il rallentamento dei mutui per l’acquisto di abitazioni.

articles.body:
China's commerce ministry did not say whether any agreements were reached, only that both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues.

BEIJING: China and the United States discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at their first trade council meeting on Friday (Nov 13), China's Commerce Ministry said on Saturday, days ahead of an expected leaders' meeting in Shenzhen next week.

"The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the outcomes of previous China-US economic and trade talks, including tariffs, a reciprocal 'US$30 billion-for-US$30 billion' tariff-cut arrangement, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern," the ministry said.

It did not say whether any agreements were reached. Both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues, the ministry added.

Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, but the plan has yet to be finalised.

Chinese purchases of US farm goods other than soybeans are on track to hit a seven-year low this year, despite an agreement to buy US$17 billion annually through 2028, a Reuters analysis of customs data showed earlier this month, underscoring persistent uncertainty over the deal.

Beijing has repeatedly urged Washington to implement the US$60 billion tariff-reduction deal, calling it a prerequisite for increasing purchases of US farm goods.

The White House said Trump will meet Xi on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen.
